<!-- introthm-1: body_md -->
\label{IntroThm} Let $k$ be an infinite field, and let $X$ be a quasi-projective $k$-scheme. Let $d={\operatorname{\rm dim}}_kX$ and suppose that  $X(d)^0$ is reduced.   Let $X^*$ be a  closed subset of $X$ such that $X\setminus X^*$ is a dense open subset of  $X_{\operatorname{reg}}(d)$. Then 
\begin{enumerate}
\item The restriction of $c_d: K_0(X)\to {\operatorname{CH}}^d(X, X^*)$ to $F^dK_0(X)$ is a group homomorphism
\[
c_d:F^dK_0(X)\to {\operatorname{CH}}^d(X, X^*).
\]
\item The cycle class map ${\rm cl}^d:{\operatorname{CH}}^d(X, X^*)\to F^dK_0(X)$ is surjective.
\item We have
\[
{\rm cl}^d\circ c_d=(-1)^{d-1}(d-1)!{\operatorname{\rm Id}}_{F^dK_0(X)}
\]
and
\[
c_d\circ {\rm cl}^d=(-1)^{d-1}(d-1)!{\operatorname{\rm Id}}_{ {\operatorname{CH}}^d(X, X^*)}.
\]
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end introthm-1 -->
<!-- introcor-1: body_md -->
\label{IntroCor} Let $k$ be an infinite field, and let $X$ be a  quasi-projective $k$-scheme. Let $d={\operatorname{\rm dim}}_kX$ and suppose that  $X(d)^0$ is reduced.  Let $X^*$ be a closed subset with $X\setminus X^*$ a dense open subset of $X_{\operatorname{reg}}(d)$. Then 
\[
{\rm cl}^d:{\operatorname{CH}}^d(X, X^*)\to F^dK_0(X)
\]
is a surjective group homomorphism with kernel killed by $(d-1)!$
<!-- end introcor-1 -->
<!-- introremark-1: body_md -->
We  use codimension $d$ rather than dimension zero as the basis for our group of cycles since the target of the Chern class $c_d$ is naturally built out of codimension $d$ cycles, while if $X$ has additional components of dimension $<d$, some 0-cycles supported in the regular locus of $X$ will have codimension $<d$. Our ultimate goal of having a Riemann-Roch theorem for our cycle group forces us to use the group ${\operatorname{CH}}^d(X, X^*)$ rather than the construction ${\operatorname{CH}}_0(X, Y)$ of \cite{LW}.

In fact, the Chow group ${\operatorname{CH}}_0(X,Y)$ may have some poor properties if $X$ is not equi-dimensional over $k$, see Example~\ref{ex:CH0} below for one such case.
<!-- end introremark-1 -->
<!-- intronotconv-1: body_md -->
1. Throughout this paper, $k$ will be a field. We let ${\operatorname{\mathbf{Sch}}}_k$ denote the category of separated schemes of finite type over $k$ and let ${\operatorname{\mathbf{Sch}}}^{\operatorname{\text{\rm qp}}}_k$ denote the full subcategory of quasi-projective $k$-schemes. Unless noted otherwise, all morphisms are assumed to be in ${\operatorname{\mathbf{Sch}}}_k$.\\[2pt]
 2. For $Y$ a scheme, we often consider only the underlying topological space of $Y$, speaking for example of open or closed subsets of $Y$.   For $Z$ a closed subscheme of $Y$, the {\em support} of $Z$, ${\rm supp}\,(Z)$, is $Z$, considered as a closed subset of $Y$, and we say that $Z$ is supported in a closed subset $Y_0$ of $Y$ if  ${\rm supp}\,(Z)\subset Y_0$.\\[2pt]
 3. Let $Y$ be a finite-type $k$ scheme. If $Y$ is integral, we define ${\operatorname{\rm dim}}_kY$ to be the transcendence dimension of $k(Y)$ over $k$, which is the same as the Krull dimension of $Y$. For $y\in Y$, define ${\operatorname{\rm dim}}_k(Y,y)$ to be the maximum of ${\operatorname{\rm dim}}_kY'$ as $Y'$ runs over the integral components of $Y$ containing $y$, and define ${\operatorname{\rm dim}}_kY:={\operatorname{\rm max}}_{y\in Y}{\operatorname{\rm dim}}_k(Y,y)$, i.e., the maximum of ${\operatorname{\rm dim}}_kY'$ as $Y'$ runs over the integral components of $Y$. If ${\operatorname{\rm dim}}_kY=d$, we say $Y$ has dimension $d$, and we say $Y$ has pure dimension $d$ if ${\operatorname{\rm dim}}_k(Y,y)=d$ for all $y\in Y$; we also express this by saying that $Y$ is equi-dimensional of dimension $d$ over $k$.
 
 We let $Y(i)$ denote the union of the integral components $Y'$ of $Y$ with ${\operatorname{\rm dim}}_kY'=i$, $Y(\le i):=\cup_{j\le i}Y(j)$, $Y(\ge i)=\cup_{j\ge i}Y(j)$. We also have the open subschemes $Y(i)^0=Y\setminus\cup_{j\neq i}Y(j)$ of $Y$, $1=0,\ldots, {\operatorname{\rm dim}}_kY$.
 
 
  Let $Z\subset Y$ be a closed subscheme. We say $Z$ has pure codimension $c$ in $Y$ if ${\operatorname{\rm dim}}_k(Z,z)+c={\operatorname{\rm dim}}_k(Y,z)$ for all $z\in Z$, and we say that $Z$ has codimension $\ge c$ in $Y$ if for each $z\in Z$, we have ${\operatorname{\rm dim}}_k(Z,z)+c\le {\operatorname{\rm dim}}_k(Y,z)$. Note that $Z=\0$ if $Z$ has codimension $\ge {\operatorname{\rm dim}}_kY+1$. \\[2pt]
 4. For $Y\in {\operatorname{\mathbf{Sch}}}_k$, line bundles $L_1,\ldots, L_r$ on $Y$ with invertible sheaves of sections ${\mathcal L}_1,\ldots, {\mathcal L}_r$ and sections $s_i\in H^0(Y, {\mathcal L}_i)$, $i=1,\ldots, r$, the zero-subscheme $V(s_1,\ldots, s_r)$ is defined as the pullback in the Cartesian square
 \[
 \xymatrix{
 V(s_1,\ldots, s_r)\ar[r]\ar[d]&Y\ar[d]^0\\
 Y\ar[r]^-{(s_1,\ldots, s_r)}&L_1\times_Y\ldots\times_YL_r
 }
 \]
If ${\mathcal I}$ is an ideal sheaf in ${\mathcal O}_Y$ and $s_i\in H^0(Y, {\mathcal I}\otimes{\mathcal L}_i)$, we define $V(s_1,\ldots, s_r)$ as above, considering $s_i$ as sections of ${\mathcal L}_i$, so $V(s_1,\ldots, s_r)\supset {\rm Spec\,}_{{\mathcal O}_Y}{\mathcal O}_Y/{\mathcal I}$.\\[2pt]
5. Let $W\subset Y$ be a closed subscheme of a $Y\in {\operatorname{\mathbf{Sch}}}_k$. We call $W$ a local complete intersection on $Y$ if the inclusion $i_W:W\to Y$ is a regular embedding, that is, for each $w\in W$, the ideal ${\mathcal I}_{W,w}\subset {\mathcal O}_{Y,w}$ is generated by a regular sequence. If $Y={\rm Spec\,} A$ is affine, we call $W$ a complete intersection in $Y$ if the ideal $I_W\subset A$ is of the form $I_W=(a_1,\ldots, a_d)$ with $a_1,\ldots, a_d$ a regular sequence in ${\mathcal O}_{Y,w}$ for each $w\in W$.
<!-- end intronotconv-1 -->
<!-- definition-1: body_md -->
Take $X\in{\operatorname{\mathbf{Sch}}}^{\operatorname{\text{\rm qp}}}_k$.  Let  $d={\operatorname{\rm dim}}_kX$ and suppose that the open subscheme $X(d)^0$ of $X$ is reduced. \\[5pt]
1. Let $X_{\operatorname{reg}}\subset X$ denote the regular locus of $X$ over $k$, that is $x\in X$ is in $X_{\operatorname{reg}}$ if and only if the local ring ${\mathcal O}_{X,x}$ is a regular local ring. Since $X$ is  of finite type over a field, $X_{\operatorname{reg}}$ is an  open subscheme of $X$. We can write $X_{\operatorname{reg}}$ as a disjoint union
\[
X_{\operatorname{reg}}=\amalg_{i=0}^dX_{\operatorname{reg}}(i),
\]
with $X_{\operatorname{reg}}(i)$ open in  $X(i)^0$;  $X_{\operatorname{reg}}(i)$ is regular of pure dimension $i$ over $k$ or is empty. If $X(i)^0$ is reduced, then $X_{\operatorname{reg}}(i)$ is dense in  $X(i)^0$, in particular  $X_{\operatorname{reg}}(d)$ is dense in $X(d)^0$. For these facts, see Lemma~\ref{lem: ReducedRegOpen} below.

Let $X_{\operatorname{sm}}\subset X_{\operatorname{reg}}$ denote the smooth locus, 
\[
x\in X_{\operatorname{sm}}\Leftrightarrow  \Omega_{X/k, x}\text{ is a free ${\mathcal O}_{X,x}$-module of rank }{\operatorname{\rm dim}}_k(X,x). 
\]
$X_{\operatorname{sm}}$ is an open subscheme of $X_{\operatorname{reg}}$ and is a disjoint union
\[
X_{\operatorname{sm}}=\amalg_{i=0}^dX_{\operatorname{sm}}(i),
\]
with $X_{\operatorname{sm}}(i)$ smooth of pure  dimension $i$ over $k$.\\[5pt]
2. Let $X_{\rm sing}:=X\setminus X_{\operatorname{reg}}$, which we call the singular locus of $X$,  and let $X^{(d)}_{\rm sing}:=X\setminus X_{\operatorname{reg}}(d)$.\\[5pt]
3. Let $X_{\operatorname{C-M}}\subset X(d)^0$ be the Cohen-Macaulay locus in $X(d)^0$.\\[5pt]
4. For $Y\in {\operatorname{\mathbf{Sch}}}_k$, and an integer $n\ge0$, let $Z_n(Y)$ be the free abelian group on the integral closed subschemes of dimension $n$ over $k$, and $Z^n(Y)$ the free abelian group on the integral closed subschemes of pure codimension $n$ in $Y$.
<!-- end definition-1 -->
<!-- lemma-1: body_md -->
\label{lem: ReducedRegOpen} For $X\in {\operatorname{\mathbf{Sch}}}_k$, $X_{\operatorname{reg}}\subset X$ is open. If $X$ is reduced, then  $X_{\operatorname{reg}}$ is dense in $X$.
<!-- end lemma-1 -->
<!-- proof-1: body_md -->
Recall that a scheme $Y$ is said  be J-2 if for every  morphism $f:Z\to Y$, locally of finite type,   the regular locus $Z_{\operatorname{reg}}$ in $Z$ is open in $Z$. By \cite[\href{https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/07R5}{tag 07R5}]{stacks-project} $k$ is J-2, so for each $Z\in {\operatorname{\mathbf{Sch}}}_k$, $Z_{\operatorname{reg}}\subset Z$ is open.  

Let $x\in X$ be a generic point. If $X$ is reduced, the local ring ${\mathcal O}_{X,x}$ is a field, hence a regular ring, so $x$ is in $X_{\operatorname{reg}}$. Thus $X_{\operatorname{reg}}$ is an open subscheme of $X$ containing each generic point, hence is dense in $X$.
<!-- end proof-1 -->
<!-- remark-1: body_md -->
\label{rem:Prelims}  Take $X\in{\operatorname{\mathbf{Sch}}}^{\operatorname{\text{\rm qp}}}_k$, let   $d={\operatorname{\rm dim}}_kX$ and suppose that $X(d)^0$ is reduced.\\[5pt]
1. $X^{(d)}_{\rm sing}=X_{\rm sing}\cup X(\le d-1)$.\\[2pt]
2. $X_{\operatorname{reg}}(d)=(X(d)^0)_{\operatorname{reg}}$, hence $X_{\operatorname{reg}}(d)$ is open in $X(d)$ and $X(d)_{\rm sing}\subset X_{\rm sing}\subset X^{(d)}_{\rm sing}$.\\[2pt]
3. By \cite[\href{https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/00RF}{Tag 00RF}]{stacks-project},  $X_{\operatorname{C-M}}$ is an open subset of $X(d)^0$, hence $X_{\operatorname{C-M}}$ is also open in $X$. Since we are assuming that $X(d)^0$ is reduced, each local ring ${\mathcal O}_{X,x}$ has depth $\ge1$, and thus the complement of $X_{\operatorname{C-M}}$ in $X(d)^0$ has codimension at least two; as $X(d)\setminus X(d)^0$ has codimension $\ge2$ in $X(d)$,   $X(d)\setminus X_{\operatorname{C-M}}$ in $X(d)$ has codimension at least two and $X(d)\setminus X_{\operatorname{C-M}}\subset X_{\rm sing}$.  \\[2pt]
4. In general $X_{\operatorname{sm}}\subset X_{\operatorname{reg}}$, and the two are equal if $k$ is perfect. For $k\subset L$ a field extension, $(X\times_kL)_{\operatorname{sm}}=(X_{\operatorname{sm}})\times_kL$. The same holds for $X_{\operatorname{reg}}$ if $L$ is separable over $k$, but not in general.
<!-- end remark-1 -->
<!-- definition-2: body_md -->
A pair $(Y, Y^*)$ consisting of a  quasi-projective $k$-scheme $Y$  and a closed subset $Y^*$ of $Y$ is called an {\em admissible pair over $k$} if  $Y({\operatorname{\rm dim}}_kY)^0$ is reduced and $Y\setminus Y^*$ is a dense open subset of $Y_{\operatorname{reg}}({\operatorname{\rm dim}}_kY)$.
<!-- end definition-2 -->
<!-- definition-3: body_md -->
\label{def:CartierCurve}  For $Y\in {\operatorname{\mathbf{Sch}}}_k$, let $Y^*\subset Y$ be a closed subset such that $Y\setminus Y^*$ is regular. A {\em Cartier curve} on $Y$ relative to $Y^*$ is a purely 1-dimensional closed subscheme $C$ of $Y$ such that\\[5pt]
i. $C\cap Y^*$ is a finite set.\\[2pt]
ii.  At each point $x\in C\cap Y^*$, the ideal ${\mathcal I}_{C,x}\subset {\mathcal O}_{Y,x}$ is generated by a regular sequence.
<!-- end definition-3 -->
<!-- remark-2: body_md -->
\label{rem:CartierCurve}
1. Let $C\subset Y$ be a Cartier curve on $Y$ relative to $Y^*$ and take $y\in C\cap Y^*$. Then a regular sequence in ${\mathcal O}_{Y,y}$ generating ${\mathcal I}_{C,y}$ must have length ${\operatorname{\rm dim}}_k(Y,y)-1$. Indeed, it follows from \cite[Lemma 5]{Matsumura} that if ${\mathcal I}_{C,y}$ is generated by a regular sequence of length 
 $\ell$, then
\[
 1={\operatorname{\rm dim}}{\mathcal O}_{Y,y}/{\mathcal I}_{C,y}={\operatorname{\rm dim}}{\mathcal O}_{Y,y}-\ell.
 \]   
2. Let $Y, Y^*$, $C$ and $y\in C\cap Y^*$ be as in (1) and let $Y'\subset Y$ be an integral component of $Y$ containing $y$. Suppose that $C$ has an integral component $C'$ with $C'\subset Y'$.  Then ${\operatorname{\rm dim}}_kY'={\operatorname{\rm dim}}_k(Y,y)$. Indeed, since each generic point of $C$ is contained in $Y_{\operatorname{reg}}$, $Y'$ is the unique integral component of $Y$ containing $C'$. By (1), the ${\mathcal I}_{C,y}$-depth of ${\mathcal O}_{Y,y}$ is ${\operatorname{\rm dim}}_k(Y,y)-1$ and by  \cite[Theorem 27, (15.G) Proposition]{Matsumura}, we have
\[
{\operatorname{\rm dim}}_k(Y,y)-1\le \text{depth}{\mathcal O}_{Y', C'}\le{\operatorname{\rm dim}} {\mathcal O}_{Y', C'}={\operatorname{\rm dim}}_kY'-1\le {\operatorname{\rm dim}}_k(Y,y)-1,
\]
giving equality throughout. 

In consequence, if $C$ is connected and has one irreducible component supported in $Y(i)$ for some $i$, then $C$ is supported in $Y(i)\setminus Y(\ge i+1)$.
<!-- end remark-2 -->
<!-- definition-4: body_md -->
For $C\in {\operatorname{\mathbf{Sch}}}_k$, ${\operatorname{\rm dim}}_kC=1$,   let $C_{(0)}$ denote the set of closed points of $C$. For $S\subset C_{(0)}$ a finite set of closed points, let ${\mathcal O}_{C:S}$ denote the colimit
\[
{\mathcal O}_{C:S}={\mathop{\rm colim}}_{T\subset (C_{(0)}\setminus S)}{\mathcal O}_C(C\setminus T).
\]
and let ${\mathcal O}_{C,S}$ denote the usual semi-local ring
\[
{\mathcal O}_{C,S}={\mathop{\rm colim}}_{\substack{U\subset C\text{ open,}\\ S\subset U}}{\mathcal O}_C(U).
\]
<!-- end definition-4 -->
<!-- remark-3: body_md -->
If $C$ has generic points $\eta_1,\ldots, \eta_r$, then ${\mathcal O}_{C:\0}$ is the total quotient ring $k(C)$, 
$k(C)=\prod_{i=1}^r{\mathcal O}_{C,\eta_i}$.

For $S\subset C_{(0)}$ a finite set,  let $C_S$ be the union of the integral components $C'$ of $C$ with $S\cap C'\neq\0$ and let $C^c_S\subset C$ be the open subscheme $C\setminus C_S$. Then
\[
{\mathcal O}_{C:S}={\mathcal O}_{C,S}\times k(C^c_S). 
\]
We let  $\alpha_S:{\mathcal O}_{C:S}\to k(C)$ be the localization map.
<!-- end remark-3 -->
<!-- definition-5: body_md -->
For $C\in {\operatorname{\mathbf{Sch}}}_k$ with ${\operatorname{\rm dim}}_kC=1$,  let $i: C_{\rm red}\hookrightarrow C$ be the associated reduced closed subscheme with irreducible components $C_{1,{\rm red}},\ldots, C_{r,{\rm red}}$, where $C_{i,{\rm red}}$ has generic point $\eta_i$, and let $i_j:C_{j,{\rm red}}\to C$ be the inclusion.  Then $k(C_{\rm red})=\prod_{i=1}^r k(\eta_i)$. Let $m_i$ denote the length of the local ring  ${\mathcal O}_{C,\eta_i}$ as ${\mathcal O}_{C,\eta_i}$-module. For $f\in k(C)^\times$, let $f_j$ denote the restriction of $f$ to $k(\eta_i)^\times$, considered as a rational function on $C_{j,{\rm red}}$, and define
${\operatorname{div}} f\in Z_0(C)=Z_0(C_{\rm red})$ as
\[
\sum_{j=1}^r i_{j*}m_j{\operatorname{div}} f_j, 
\]
where ${\operatorname{div}} f_j$ is the usual divisor of $f_j$ \cite[\S 1.3]{Fulton}; note that by definition, ${\operatorname{div}} f_j=0$ if  ${\operatorname{\rm dim}}_kC_{j, {\rm red}}=0$.  For $f\in {\mathcal O}_{C:S}^\times$, define ${\operatorname{div}} f={\operatorname{div}}\, \alpha_S(f)$.
<!-- end definition-5 -->
<!-- definition-6: body_md -->
\label{def:RatlEquiv} Let $(X, X^*)$ be an admissible pair. Define $R^d(X,X^*)\subset Z^d(X\setminus X^*)$ to be the subgroup generated by 0-cycles of the form $i_{C*}({\operatorname{div}} f)$, where $i_C:C\to X$ is the inclusion of a Cartier curve on $X$ relative to $X^*$, and $f$ is a unit in   ${\mathcal O}_{C: C\cap X^*}$:
\begin{multline*}
R^d(X,X^*):=\<\{i_{C*}({\operatorname{div}} f)\mid i_C:C\to X\text{ is a Cartier curve relative to }X^*,\\\text{and } f\in {\mathcal O}_{C:C\cap Y}^\times\}\>
\end{multline*}
<!-- end definition-6 -->
<!-- definition-7: body_md -->
For $(X, X^*)$ an admissible pair, define 
\[
{\operatorname{CH}}^d(X,X^*)=Z^d(X\setminus X^*)/R^d(X,X^*).
\]
<!-- end definition-7 -->
<!-- remark-4: body_md -->
For $X$ reduced, the definition of ${\operatorname{CH}}^d(X, X^*)$ given here already appears in  \cite[\S 2]{BS98} in case ${\operatorname{\rm dim}}_kX=2$, with $X^*=X_{\rm sing}\cup X(\le d-1)$ (this closed subset is denoted $X_{\rm sing}$ in {\it loc.\! cit.}), and is extended to  reduced $X$ of arbitrary dimension $d$ in \cite[\S 2]{BS99}, again with $X^*$ the minimal choice $X_{\rm sing}\cup X(\le d-1)$ (still denoted $X_{\rm sing}$ in \cite{BS99}). This definition is also used in \cite{ESV}.  In \cite{BS99}, they kindly cite \cite{LW} as source, even though this definition does not really appear in \cite{LW} as such, unless $X$ is equi-dimensional over $k$, as we will explain below.
<!-- end remark-4 -->
<!-- definition-8: body_md -->
\label{def:LW0Cyc} 1. Let $Y$ be a finite-type separated $k$-scheme and let $Y^*$ be a closed subset such that $Y\setminus Y^*$ is regular. Let $R_0(Y, Y^*)\subset Z_0(Y\setminus Y^*)$ be the subgroup generated by 0-cycles of the form $i_{C*}({\operatorname{div}} f)$, where $i_C:C\to Y$ is the inclusion of a Cartier curve on $Y$ relative to $Y^*$ and $f\in{\mathcal O}_{C: C\cap Y^*}^\times$.\\[2pt]
2. With $Y, Y^*$ as in (1), define ${\operatorname{CH}}_0(Y, Y^*)=Z_0(Y\setminus Y^*)/R_0(Y, Y^*)$.
<!-- end definition-8 -->
<!-- remark-5: body_md -->
\label{rem:CartierCurve2} 1. Let $i_C:C\to X$ be a Cartier curve on $X$ relative to $X^*$ and take $f\in{\mathcal O}_{C:C\cap X^*}^\times$. Then the support of ${\operatorname{div}} f$ is contained in $C\setminus X^*$, so  $R^d(X,X^*)$ is indeed a subgroup of $Z^d(X\setminus X^*)$; similarly, $R_0(Y, Y^*)$ is indeed a subgroup of $Z_0(Y\setminus Y^*)$. \\[2pt]
2.  In addition to the conditions (i) and (ii) of Definition~\ref{def:CartierCurve}, the definition of Cartier curve on $Y$ relative to $Y^*$  given in, e.g., \cite{BS99} 
requires  
\\[5pt]
iii. $C$ has no embedded components in $C\cap (Y\setminus Y^*)$ and if 
$C'$ is an irreducible component of $C$ with $C'\cap Y^*=\0$, then $C'$ is reduced at its generic point.\\[5pt]
It is not hard to show that adding the requirement (iii) does not affect the resulting subgroup $R_0(Y,Y)$ of $Z_0(Y\setminus Y^*)$,  so the group ${\operatorname{CH}}_0(Y, Y^*)$ defined above agrees with that of {\it loc. cit.}  \\[2pt]
3. Since we are using codimension rather than dimension, one might think that a Cartier ``curve'' should rather be a closed subscheme $C$ of pure {\em codimension} $d-1$ on $X$,   satisfying the conditions (i) and (ii) of Definition~\ref{def:CartierCurve}. However,  such a $C$ decomposes a disjoint union
\[
C=C(d)\amalg C(d-1)
\]
where $C(d)$ is a purely one-dimensional closed subscheme of $X$, supported in $X(d)$, and $C(d-1)$ is a purely 0-dimensional closed subscheme of $X$, supported in $X(d-1)\setminus X(d)$. Then $C(d)$ is a Cartier curve relative to $X^*$ following  Definition~\ref{def:CartierCurve}. Moreover, letting $f(d)$ denote the restriction of $f$ to $C(d)$, we have
\[
i_{C*}({\operatorname{div}} f)=i_{C(d)*}({\operatorname{div}} f(d)),
\]
since ${\operatorname{\rm dim}}_kX(d-1)=0$. Thus,  we end up with the same subgroup $R^d(X, X^*)$ whether we use purely dimension one closed subschemes or purely codimension $d-1$ closed subschemes to define $R^d(X, X^*)$; we can even omit the condition (ii) at points of $C(d-1)\subset X(d-1)\setminus X(d)$.
\\[2pt]
4. Suppose $X$ has connected components $X_1,\ldots, X_s$ and let $X^*_j=X^*\cap X_j$. Suppose that ${\operatorname{\rm dim}}_kX_j={\operatorname{\rm dim}}_kX$  for $j=1,\ldots, r$ and ${\operatorname{\rm dim}}_kX_j<{\operatorname{\rm dim}}_kX$  for $j=r+1,\ldots, s$. Then
\[
{\operatorname{CH}}^d(X, X^*)=\oplus_{j=1}^r{\operatorname{CH}}^d(X_j, X_j^*)
\]
For this reason we often assume that $X$ is connected.
<!-- end remark-5 -->
<!-- proposition-1: body_md -->
\label{prop:Comparison} Let $(X, X^*)$ be an admissible pair with $X$ of dimension $d$ over $k$ and let $Y^*\subset X^*$ be a closed subset such that $X\setminus Y^*$ is regular. \\[5pt]
1.  If $Y^*\cap X(d)=X^*\cap X(d)$, then $j^{X^*,Y^*}_*$ is injective\\[2pt]
2. If   $Y^*=X^*$, then $j^{X^*,Y^*}_*$ is an isomorphism.
<!-- end proposition-1 -->
<!-- proof-2: body_md -->
It follows immediately from the definitions that, after identifying $Z^d(X\setminus X^*)$ with $Z_0(X\setminus X^*)$, we have $R^d(X, X^*)=R_0(X, X^*)$, proving (2).

For (1), if a zero-cycle $z\in Z^d(X\setminus X^*)=Z_0(X\setminus X^*)$ goes to zero in ${\operatorname{CH}}_0(X, Y^*)$, there are Cartier curves $C_1,\ldots, C_s$ on $X$ relative to $Y^*$ and functions $f_j\in {\mathcal O}_{C_j: C_j\cap Y}^\times$, $j=1,\ldots, s$, such that
\[
z=\sum_{j=1}^si_{C_j*}{\operatorname{div}}(f_j).
\]
We may assume that each $C_j$ is connected. 

Suppose that $C_1,\ldots, C_r$ each have some integral component supported in $X(d)$, and $C_{r+1},\ldots, C_s$ are all supported in $X(\le d-1)$. By Remark~\ref{rem:CartierCurve}(2), $C_i$ is supported in $X(d)$ for $i=1,\ldots, r$ and $C_i$ is supported in $X(\le d-1)\setminus X(d)$ for $i=r+1,\ldots, s$. Thus 
\[
z=\sum_{j=1}^ri_{C_j*}{\operatorname{div}}(f_j).
\]
Since $C_j$ is a Cartier curve relative to $Y^*$ and $Y^*\cap X(d)=X^*\cap X(d)$ by assumption, we see that  $C_j$ is a Cartier curve relative to $X^*$ for $j=1,\ldots, r$, and thus $[z]=0$ in ${\operatorname{CH}}^d(X, X^*)$, showing that $j^{X^*, Y^*}_*$ is injective.
<!-- end proof-2 -->
<!-- remark-6: body_md -->
\label{rem:Comparison2} Following the argument used in the proof of Proposition~\ref{prop:Comparison}, we see that the subgroup of relations $R_0(X, Y^*)$ is a direct sum
\[
R_0(X, Y^*)=R^d(X, Y^*\cup X(\le d-1))\oplus R_0'(X(\le d-1), Y^*\cap X(\le d-1))
\]
where 
\[
R_0'(X(\le d-1), Y^*\cap X(\le d-1))\subset R_0(X(\le d-1), Y^*\cap X(\le d-1))
\]
is the subgroup generated by 0-cycles of the form $i_{C*}({\operatorname{div}} f)$, with  $i_C:C\to X(\le d-1)$ a Cartier curve relative to $Y^*\cap X(\le d-1)$ such that $C\cap X(d)=\0$, with $f\in {\mathcal O}_{C: C\cap Y^*}^\times$. 

This refines Proposition~\ref{prop:Comparison} to give the description of ${\operatorname{CH}}_0(X, Y^*)$ as
\begin{multline*}
{\operatorname{CH}}_0(X, Y^*)={\operatorname{CH}}^d(X, Y^*\cup X(\le d-1))\\\oplus Z_0(X(\le d-1)\setminus Y^*)/R_0'(X(\le d-1), Y^*\cap X(\le d-1)).
\end{multline*}
<!-- end remark-6 -->
<!-- ex-1: body_md -->
\label{ex:CH0} Let $X={\rm Spec\,} k[x,y,z]/(z(x,y))$, so $X$ is the union of the $x$-$y$-plane with the $z$-axis. We take $Y^*$ to be the origin. Since a curve supported in $X(\le 1)$ must contain $Y^*=X(\le1)\cap X(2)$, it follows that the group of relations $R_0'(z\text{-axis}, \{(0,0,0)\})$ is zero and  as ${\operatorname{CH}}^2(X, z\text{-axis})=0$, we have
\[
{\operatorname{CH}}_0(X, \{(0,0,0)\})=Z_0(z\text{-axis}\setminus\{(0,0,0\}).
\]
<!-- end ex-1 -->
<!-- remark-7: body_md -->
\label{rem:CH1=Pic} Let $(X, X^*)$ be an admissible pair with $X$ of pure dimension one. Then sending a closed point $x\in X\setminus X^*$ to the invertible sheaf ${\mathcal O}_X(x)$ induces an isomorphism
\[
{\rm cl}^1:{\operatorname{CH}}^1(X, X^*)\xrightarrow{\sim} {\rm Pic}(X)
\]
After identifying  ${\operatorname{CH}}^1(X, X^*)$ with ${\operatorname{CH}}_0(X, X^*)$, this is proven in \cite[Proposition 1.4]{LW}.
<!-- end remark-7 -->
<!-- remark-8: body_md -->
Let $Y\in {\operatorname{\mathbf{Sch}}}_k$ be a Cohen-Macaulay scheme, that is, ${\mathcal O}_{Y,y}$ is a Cohen-Macaulay local ring for each $y\in Y$, see \cite[(16.A)]{Matsumura}. Let $W\subset Y$ be a closed subscheme of pure codimension $c>0$. Then $W$ is a local complete intersection on $Y$ if and only if the ideal ${\mathcal I}_{W,w}\subset {\mathcal O}_{Y,w}$ is generated by $c$ elements for each $w\in W$. Indeed, since ${\mathcal O}_{Y,w}$ is Cohen-Macaulay, elements $s_1,\ldots, s_c$ in the maximal ideal $\mathfrak{m}_w\subset {\mathcal O}_{Y,w}$ form a regular sequence if and only if the ideal $(s_1,\ldots, s_c)$ has height $c$ \cite[Theorem 31]{Matsumura}.

We will be using this fact without further comment throughout the paper.
<!-- end remark-8 -->
<!-- lemma-2: body_md -->
\label{lem:CHSurj} Let $(X, X^*)$, $(X, X')$ be admissible pairs with $X'\subset X^*$. Let $d={\operatorname{\rm dim}}_kX$. Then the map
\[
j^{X^*, X'}_*:{\operatorname{CH}}^d(X, X^*)\to {\operatorname{CH}}^d(X, X')
\]
 is surjective.
<!-- end lemma-2 -->
<!-- proof-3: body_md -->
Take a closed point $x\in X^*\setminus X'$ and note that $x$ is in $X_{\operatorname{reg}}(d)$. It suffices to show that $[x]\in {\operatorname{CH}}^d(X, X')$ is in the image of $j^{X^*, X'}_*:{\operatorname{CH}}^d(X, X^*)\to {\operatorname{CH}}^d(X, X')$. For this, choose a locally closed immersion $X\subset {\mathbb P}^N$ and let $C\subset X(d)$ be a general  intersection in $X(d)$ of $d-1$ hypersurfaces of large degree $e$, containing $y$. Taking $e\gg0$, we may assume that 
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(a)] $C$ is of pure codimension $d-1$ on $X(d)$.
\item[(b)] $x$ is a regular point of $C$.
\item[(c)]   $C\cap X^*$ is a finite set 
\item[(d)]  $C$ is contained in $X_{\operatorname{C-M}}$.
\end{enumerate}
Note that $X^*$ has dimension $\le d-1$ and  $X(d)\setminus X_{\operatorname{C-M}}$  has dimension $\le d-2$ (see Remark~\ref{rem:Prelims}  above), which is why we may assume that (c) and (d) hold.

Since $X_{\operatorname{C-M}}\subset X(d)^0$, it follows from (a) and (d) that $C$ is locally defined by a regular sequence of length $d-1$ as a closed subscheme of $X$, and hence by (c), $C$ is a Cartier curve relative to $X^*$. By (b) and the usual arguments using the Chinese remainder theorem, we may find an $f\in {\mathcal O}_{C: C\cap X'}^\times$ such that $i_{C*}({\operatorname{div}} f)=1\cdot x-y$ with $y$ supported in $X\setminus X^*$. This gives us the class $[y]\in {\operatorname{CH}}^d(X, X^*)$ with $1\cdot x-y$ in $R^d(X, X')$, hence $[x]=j^{X^*, X'}_*([y])$ in ${\operatorname{CH}}^d(X, X')$.
<!-- end proof-3 -->
<!-- definition-9: body_md -->
1. Let $(X, X^*)$ be an admissible pair. Let $S\subset X$ be a closed subset and let $C$ be a Cartier curve on $X$ relative to $X^*$. We say that $C$ is {\em $S$-strict} if $C\cap S=\0$.\\[2pt]
2. Let $R^d(X, X^*)_S\subset R^d(X, X^*)$ be the subgroup generated by $i_{C*}({\operatorname{div}} f)$ with $C$ an $S$-strict Cartier curve on $X$ relative to $X^*$, and $f\in {\mathcal O}_{C: C\cap X^*}^\times$.\\[2pt]
3. Define
\[
 R^d(X, X^*)^{\operatorname{C-M}}:= R^d(X, X^*)_{X(d)\setminus X_{\operatorname{C-M}}}
\]
<!-- end definition-9 -->
<!-- lemma-3: body_md -->
\label{lem:MovingLemmaR0} Take $X\in {\operatorname{\mathbf{Sch}}}_k^{\operatorname{\text{\rm qp}}}$, let $d={\operatorname{\rm dim}}_kX$, and suppose $X(d)^0$ is reduced.  Let $Y^*\subset X$ be a closed subset such that $X\setminus Y^*$ is regular and $X(d)\setminus Y^*$ is dense in $X(d)$. Let $S\subset Y^*\cap X(d)$ be a closed subset such that ${\rm codim}_{X(d)}S\ge 2$.  Let $i_C:C\to X$ be a Cartier curve on $X$ relative to $Y^*$ such that $C$ is supported in $X(d)$, and take $f\in {\mathcal O}_{C: C\cap Y^*}^\times$. Then there are Cartier curves on $X$ relative to $Y^*$, $i_{C_j}:C_j\to X$, and $f_j\in {\mathcal O}_{C_j: C_j\cap Y^*}^\times$, $j=1,\ldots, s$, such that each $C_j$ is supported in $X(d)$, $C_j\cap S=\0$,  and we have
\[
i_{C*}({\operatorname{div}} f)=\sum_{j=1}^si_{C_j*}({\operatorname{div}} f_j).
\]
<!-- end lemma-3 -->
<!-- proof-4: body_md -->
If we write $C=C'\cup C''$ where   $C''$ is disjoint from $Y^*$, then clearly  $C''$ is an $S$-strict Cartier curve relative to $Y^*$, $f_{|C''}$ is in ${\mathcal O}_{C'': C''\cap Y^*}^\times=k(C'')^\times$, $f_{|C'}$ is in ${\mathcal O}_{C': C'\cap Y^*}^\times$ and
\[
i_{C*}({\operatorname{div}} f)=i_{C'*}({\operatorname{div}} f_{|C'})+i_{C''*}({\operatorname{div}} f_{|C'}).
\]
Thus we may assume from the start that each irreducible component of $C$ intersects $Y^*$. 

By assumption $C$ is supported in $X(d)$ and there is an affine open neighborhood $U$ of the finite set $C\cap Y^*$ in $X$ such that ${\mathcal I}_C$ is defined by a regular sequence $g_1,\ldots, g_{d-1}$ on $U$, equivalently, the images of $g_1,\ldots, g_{d-1}$ in ${\mathcal I}_C/{\mathcal I}_C^2$ generate this sheaf on $U$.  Letting ${\mathcal O}_X(1)$ be a very ample invertible sheaf on $X$, we may assume that the $g_i$ extend to global sections $g_i\in H^0(X, {\mathcal I}_C(m))$ for some $m\gg0$. Again taking $m\gg0$, we may assume that $H^0(X, {\mathcal I}_C(m))$ generates ${\mathcal I}_C(m)$ globally. Thus we may assume that the linear system defined by $H^0(X, {\mathcal I}_C(m))$ has only $C$ as base-locus. Since $k$ is infinite, we may assume that 
\[
{\rm codim}_{S\setminus C} V(g_1,\ldots, g_i)\cap (S\setminus C)\ge i
\]
for each $i=1,\ldots, d-1$. But since ${\operatorname{\rm dim}} S\le d-2$, it follows that we may choose $g_1,\ldots, g_{d-1}$ such that  $V(g_1,\ldots, g_{d-1})\cap (S\setminus C)=\0$. 

Similarly, we may assume that 
\[
{\rm codim}_{Y^*\setminus C} V(g_1,\ldots, g_i)\cap (Y^*\setminus C)\ge i
\]
for each $i=1,\ldots, d-1$. In particular,  $V(g_1,\ldots, g_{d-1})\setminus C$ is disjoint from $X(i)$ for  $i<d-1$. Also, since $X(d-1)\cap X(j)$ has codimension $\ge2$ in $X$ for all $j\neq d-1$, we may assume that $V(g_1,\ldots, g_{d-1})\cap X(d-1)\setminus C$ is a finite set contained in $X(d-1)^0$.
Letting 
\[
\tilde{X}_{\operatorname{C-M}}=X_{\operatorname{C-M}}\amalg X(d-1)^0.
\]
we may therefore assume that $V(g_1,\ldots, g_{d-1})\setminus C\subset \tilde{X}_{\operatorname{C-M}}$, and that $V(g_1,\ldots, g_{d-1})\setminus C$ has pure codimension $d-1$ in $\tilde{X}_{\operatorname{C-M}}\setminus C$.  Since $C$ is supported in $X(d)$, $V(g_1,\ldots, g_{d-1})\setminus C$ is the disjoint union of closed subschemes,
\[
V(g_1,\ldots, g_{d-1})\setminus C=(V(g_1,\ldots, g_{d-1})\setminus C)_{\operatorname{C-M}}\amalg V(g_1,\ldots, g_{d-1})_{d-1},
\]
with $(V(g_1,\ldots, g_{d-1})\setminus C)_{\operatorname{C-M}}\subset X_{\operatorname{C-M}}$ and 
$V(g_1,\ldots, g_{d-1})_{d-1}\subset  X(d-1)^0$. Similarly,  
\[
V(g_1,\ldots, g_{d-1})=V(g_1,\ldots, g_{d-1})_d\amalg V(g_1,\ldots, g_{d-1})_{d-1}
\]
with $V(g_1,\ldots, g_{d-1})_d$ supported in $X(d)$.  Since $X_{\operatorname{C-M}}$ is Cohen-Macaulay, it follows that $g_1\ldots, g_{d-1}$ is a regular sequence at each point of $(V(g_1,\ldots, g_{d-1})\setminus C)_{\operatorname{C-M}}$. 



Since $C\setminus Y^*$ has pure codimension $d-1$ on $X\setminus Y^*$ and is contained in $X_{\operatorname{reg}}(d)$, we may also assume that  $V(g_1,\ldots, g_{d-1})\setminus (Y^*\cap C)$ has pure codimension $d-1$ in $X\setminus (Y^*\cap C)$, so   $g_1\ldots, g_{d-1}$ is a regular sequence at each point of $V(g_1,\ldots, g_{d-1})_d\setminus (Y^*\cap C)$. But since $g_1\ldots, g_{d-1}$ is also a regular sequence on $U$, it follows that $g_1\ldots, g_{d-1}$ is a regular sequence at each point of $V(g_1,\ldots, g_{d-1})_d$.  

Letting $E$ be the closure of 
$V(g_1,\ldots, g_{d-1})_d \setminus C$ in $X$, the assumption that $g_1,\ldots, g_{d-1}$ generates ${\mathcal I}_C$ on $U$ shows that $E\cap C\subset X(d)\setminus U$. As $V(g_1,\ldots, g_{d-1})_{d-1}$ is a finite set disjoint from $X(d)$, we may assume that $U\cap V(g_1,\ldots, g_{d-1})_{d-1}=\0$, hence 
\[
V(g_1,\ldots, g_{d-1})\cap U=(C\cap U)\amalg (E\cap U),
\]
 in particular, 
\[
E\cap C\cap Y^*=\0,\ E\cap S=\0,
\]
$E$ is supported in $X(d)$, and is a local complete intersection on $U\cup (X\setminus C)$.  Since $Y^*\subset U\cup (X\setminus C)$,   we see that $E$ is an $S$-strict Cartier curve on $X$, supported in $X(d)$. 

Replacing $g_{d-1}$ with a sufficiently general element $g_{d-1}'\in H^0(X, {\mathcal O}_X(m))$, we may assume as above that 
\[
V(g_1,\ldots, g_{d-1}')=V(g_1,\ldots, g_{d-1}')\cap X_{\operatorname{C-M}}\amalg V(g_1,\ldots, g_{d-1}')\cap X(d-1)^0,
\]
writing  $V(g_1,\ldots, g_{d-1}')$ as
\[
V(g_1,\ldots, g_{d-1}')=V(g_1,\ldots, g_{d-1}')_{\operatorname{C-M}}\amalg V(g_1,\ldots, g_{d-1}')_{d-1}.
\]
Let $E'=V(g_1,\ldots, g_{d-2},g_{d-1}')_{\operatorname{C-M}}$. Arguing as above, $E'$ is a closed subscheme of $X$, $g_1,\ldots, g_{d-2}, g_{d-1}'$  is a regular sequence  at each point of $E'$, and $E'$ is an $S$-strict Cartier curve on $X$ relative to $Y^*$. We may also chose $g_{d-1}'$ so that ${\operatorname{div}} g_{d-1}$ and ${\operatorname{div}} g_{d-1}'$ have no common components in $X$, giving the well-defined rational function $g_{d-1}/g_{d-1}'$ on $X$.

We may write the rational function $f\in {\mathcal O}_{C: C\cap Y^*}^\times$ as the restriction to $C$ of a fraction $f_0/f_\infty$, with  $f_0, f_\infty\in H^0(X, {\mathcal O}_X(n))$ for some $n\gg0$ and with $f_0, f_\infty$ restricting to ${\mathcal O}_{X, C\cap Y^*}^\times$ (after trivializing ${\mathcal O}_X(n)$ in a neighborhood of $C\cap Y^*$.  As we may modify $f_0, f_\infty$ by adding any element $g\in H^0(X, {\mathcal I}_C(n))$, we may argue as above to show that we may choose $f_0, f_\infty$ so that ${\operatorname{div}}(f_0)$ and ${\operatorname{div}}(f_\infty)$ have no common components on $X$, so we have the well-defined rational function $f_0/f_\infty$ on $X$, and in addition:
\\[5pt]
a. $V(g_1,\ldots, g_{d-2}, f_0)$ and $V(g_1,\ldots, g_{d-2}, f_\infty)$ have pure codimension $d-1$ on $X$, and are supported in $X_{\operatorname{C-M}}\amalg X(d-1)^0$, writing them as above as
\[
V(g_1,\ldots, g_{d-2}, f_i)=V(g_1,\ldots, g_{d-2}, f_i)_{\operatorname{C-M}}\amalg V(g_1,\ldots, g_{d-2}, f_i)_{d-1}
\]
for $i\in \{0, \infty\}$.\\[2pt]
b. $g_1,\ldots, g_{d-2}, f_0$,  is a regular sequence at each point of $V(g_1,\ldots, g_{d-2}, f_0)_{\operatorname{C-M}}$, and  $g_1,\ldots, g_{d-2}, f_\infty$ is a regular sequence at each point of  $V(g_1,\ldots, g_{d-2}, f_\infty)_{\operatorname{C-M}}$.\\[2pt]
c. $V(g_1,\ldots, g_{d-2}, f_0)\cap C\cap Y^*=\0$ and $V(g_1,\ldots, g_{d-2}, f_\infty)\cap C\cap Y^*=\0$.\\[2pt]
d. Let 
\[
\hat{C}:=V(g_1,\ldots, g_{d-2}, f_0)_{\operatorname{C-M}}, \ \hat{C}':=V(g_1,\ldots, g_{d-2}, f_\infty)_{\operatorname{C-M}}. 
\]
Then $\hat{C}$ and $\hat{C}'$  are supported in $X(d)$ and are $S$-strict Cartier curves on $X$, relative to $Y^*$.\\[2pt]
e. The rational function $f_0/f_\infty$ restricts to well-defined rational functions on $E$ and $E'$
\[
(f_0/f_\infty)_E\in {\mathcal O}_{E: E\cap Y^*}^\times,\ (f_0/f_\infty)_{E'}\in {\mathcal O}_{E': E'\cap Y^*}^\times
\]
f. The rational function $g_{d-1}/g_{d-1}'$ restricts to well-defined rational functions on $\hat{C}$ and $\hat{C}'$
\[
(g_{d-1}/g_{d-1}')_{\hat{C}}\in {\mathcal O}_{\hat{C}: \hat{C}\cap Y^*}^\times,\ (g_{d-1}/g_{d-1}')_{\hat{C}'}\in {\mathcal O}_{\hat{C}': \hat{C}'\cap Y^*}^\times
\]

An elementary computation shows that
\begin{multline*}
i_{C*}({\operatorname{div}} f)=i_{\hat{C}*}({\operatorname{div}} (g_{d-1}/g_{d-1}')_{\hat{C}})+i_{E*}({\operatorname{div}}(f_\infty/f_0)_E)\\+i_{E'*}({\operatorname{div}}(f_0/f_\infty)_{E'})+i_{\hat{C}'*}({\operatorname{div}} (g_{d-1}'/g_{d-1})_{\hat{C}'}).
\end{multline*}
Since $E, \hat{C}, E'$ and $\hat{C}'$ are all $S$-strict Cartier curves supported in $X(d)$, this completes the proof.
<!-- end proof-4 -->
<!-- lemma-4: body_md -->
\label{lem:Mov1} Suppose that $k$ is an infinite field. Let $(X, X^*)$ be an admissible pair, let $d={\operatorname{\rm dim}}_kX$, and let $S\subset X^*\cap X(d)$ be a closed subset such that ${\rm codim}_{X(d)}S\ge2$. Then $R^d(X, X^*)_S= R^d(X, X^*)$.
<!-- end lemma-4 -->
<!-- proof-5: body_md -->
This follows directly from  Lemma~\ref{lem:MovingLemmaR0} with $Y^*=X^*$.
<!-- end proof-5 -->
<!-- proposition-2: body_md -->
\label{prop:CMMoving} Suppose that $k$ is an infinite field. Let $(X, X^*)$ be an admissible pair and let $d={\operatorname{\rm dim}}_kX$. Then   $R^d(X, X^*)=R^d(X, X^*)^{\operatorname{C-M}}$.
<!-- end proposition-2 -->
<!-- proof-6: body_md -->
This follows from Lemma~\ref{lem:Mov1}, taking $S=X(d)\setminus X_{\operatorname{C-M}}\subset  X^*\cap X(d)$.
<!-- end proof-6 -->
<!-- proposition-3: body_md -->
\label{prop:CH0CH*} Suppose $k$ is an infinite field and $X$ is reduced. Let $Y^*\subset X$ be a closed subset such that $X\setminus Y^*$ is regular  and dense in $X$, and let $X^*(\le i)=(Y^*\cap X(i))\cup X(\le i-1)$. Suppose that  
\begin{equation}\label{eqn:AssumptionCH0CH*}
{\rm codim}_{X(i)}X(i)\cap X(j)\ge 2
\end{equation}
for all $0\le i<j\le {\operatorname{\rm dim}}_kX$. Then the map $\gamma_{X, Y^*}$ in  \eqref{eqn:CH0CH*Comp} is an isomorphism.
<!-- end proposition-3 -->
<!-- proof-7: body_md -->
Let $d={\operatorname{\rm dim}}_kX$. By  Remark~\ref{rem:Comparison2}, we have
\begin{multline*}
{\operatorname{CH}}_0(X, Y^*)={\operatorname{CH}}^d(X, X^*(\le d))\\\oplus 
Z_0(X(\le d-1)\setminus Y^*)/R_0'(X(\le d-1), Y^*\cap X(\le d-1)),
\end{multline*}
where we recall that 
\[
R_0'(X(\le d-1), Y^*\cap X(\le d-1))\subset R_0(X(\le d-1), Y^*\cap X(\le d-1))
\]
 is the subgroup generated by 0-cycles of the form $i_{C*}({\operatorname{div}} f)$, where $i_C:C\to X(\le d-1)$ is a Cartier curve relative to $Y^*\cap X(\le d-1)$, $f\in {\mathcal O}_{C: C\cap Y^*}^\times$ and $C\cap X(d)=\0$.



Assuming \eqref{eqn:AssumptionCH0CH*}, we claim that 
\begin{equation}\label{eqn:ClaimR'=R}
R_0'(X(\le d-1), Y^*\cap X(\le d-1))=R_0(X(\le d-1), Y^*\cap X(\le d-1)).
\end{equation}
For this, consider a connected Cartier curve $i_C:C\to X(\le d-1)$ on $X(\le d-1)$, relative to $Y^*\cap X(\le d-1)$ and function $f\in {\mathcal O}_{C: C\cap Y^*}^\times$. By Remark~\ref{rem:CartierCurve}(2), $C$ is supported in $X(i)$ for some $i\le d-1$ and $C\cap \cup_{j=i+1}^{d-1}X(j)=\0$; in particular $C$ is a Cartier curve on $X(\le i)$ and $f\in {\mathcal O}_{C: C\cap Y^*\cap X(\le i)}^\times$. Moreover $Y^*\cap X(i)\supset X(i)\cap X(\ge i+1)$, and $X(i)\cap X(\ge i+1)$ has codimension $\ge 2$ on  $X(i)$. We apply Lemma~\ref{lem:MovingLemmaR0} (with $X=X(\le i)$, $S=X(i)\cap X(\ge i+1)$ and $Y^*\cap X(\le i)$ replacing $Y^*$). This gives us Cartier curves $\iota_j:C_j\to X(\le i)$ relative to $Y^*\cap X(\le i)$, supported on $X(i)$,  and functions $f_j\in {\mathcal O}_{C_j: C_j\cap Y^*}^\times$, $j=1,\ldots, s$, with $C_j\cap X(\ge i+1)=\0$ and
\[
i_{C*}({\operatorname{div}} f)=\sum_{j=1}^s i_{C_j*}({\operatorname{div}} f_j).
\]
But then $C_j$ is a Cartier curve on $X(\le d-1)$ relative to $Y^*\cap X(d-1)$, with $C_j\cap X(d)=\0$, hence $i_{C*}({\operatorname{div}} f)$ is in $R_0'(X(\le d-1), Y^*\cap X(\le d-1))$.

As such 0-cycles $i_{C*}({\operatorname{div}} f)$ generate $R_0(X(\le d-1), Y^*\cap X(\le d-1))$, this verifies \eqref{eqn:ClaimR'=R}, and thus 
\[
Z_0(X(\le d-1)\setminus Y^*)/R_0'(X(\le d-1), Y^*\cap X(\le d-1))={\operatorname{CH}}_0(X(\le d-1), Y^*\cap X(\le d-1))).
\]
By induction on $d$, 
\[
{\operatorname{CH}}_0(X(\le d-1), Y^*\cap X(\le d-1)))=\oplus_{i=0}^{d-1}{\operatorname{CH}}^i(X(\le i), X^*(\le i))
\]
and thus
\[
{\operatorname{CH}}_0(X, Y^*)=\oplus_{i=0}^d{\operatorname{CH}}^i(X(\le i), X^*(\le i)).
\]
<!-- end proof-7 -->
<!-- definition-10: body_md -->
\label{def:RelationsII} For an admissible pair $(X, X^*)$, let $\tilde{R}^d(X,X^*)$ be the subgroup of $Z^d(X\setminus X^*)$ generated by cycles of the form
\[
p_{1*}(|W|\cdot (X \times \{0\} - X \times \{\infty\})) \in Z^d(X\setminus X^*),
\]
where $W\subset X\times{\mathbb P}^1$ is a closed subscheme of pure dimension one, satisfying properties \eqref{eqn:Properties}(i.-iii.).
<!-- end definition-10 -->
<!-- remark-9: body_md -->
\label{rem:CodimNotDim} A closed subscheme $W$ of $X\times{\mathbb P}^1$ of pure codimension $d$  has pure dimension one support in $X(d)\times{\mathbb P}^1$, but could also have dimension zero support in $X(d-1)\times{\mathbb P}^1$. For some arguments later on, it may be useful to index via codimension rather than dimension, and allow closed subschemes $W'\subset X\times{\mathbb P}^1$ of pure codimension $d$, rather than pure dimension one. In this case, we modify \eqref{eqn:Properties}(i,ii) to: \\[5pt]
(i$'$) $W'\subset X\times{\mathbb P}^1$ has pure codimension $d$. We have $W'\subset 
(X_{\operatorname{C-M}}\amalg X(d-1)^0)\times{\mathbb P}^1$,  $W'\cap X^*\times\{0,\infty\}=\0$ and $W'\cap X^*\times{\mathbb P}^1$ is supported in a finite set.\\[2pt]
(ii$'$) In an open neighborhood of $W'\cap (X^*\cap X_{\operatorname{C-M}})\times {\mathbb P}^1$, $W'$ is defined by a regular sequence of length $d$.
\\[5pt]
and still require  \eqref{eqn:Properties}(iii.).

Given such a $W'$, note that $W'$ is a pure codimension $d$ closed subscheme of the disjoint union $X_{\operatorname{C-M}}\times{\mathbb P}^1\amalg X(d-1)^0\times{\mathbb P}^1$,  the component $W:=W'\cap X(d)\times{\mathbb P}^1=W'\cap X_{\operatorname{C-M}}\times{\mathbb P}^1$ has pure dimension one, satisfies 
\eqref{eqn:Properties}(i.-iii.) and
\[
p_{1*}(|W'|\cdot (X \times \{0\} - X \times \{\infty\}))= p_{1*}(|W|\cdot (X \times \{0\} - X \times \{\infty\}))\in Z^d(X\setminus X^*). 
\]
Thus, this change of conditions does not alter the subgroup $\tilde{R}^d(X,X^*)\subset Z^d(X\setminus X^*)$; compare with Remark~\ref{rem:CartierCurve2}.
<!-- end remark-9 -->
<!-- theorem-1: body_md -->
\label{thm:Relations} Let $(X, X^*)$ be an admissible pair and let  $d={\operatorname{\rm dim}}_kX$. Then we have $R^d(X,X^*)=\tilde{R}^d(X,X^*)$.
<!-- end theorem-1 -->
<!-- remark-10: body_md -->
\label{rem:CaseDim1} For an admissible pair $(X, X^*)$ with $X$ of dimension one, Theorem~\ref{thm:Relations}  is classical. If we write $X=X_0\amalg X_1$, it is easy to see that 
Theorem~\ref{thm:Relations} for $(X_1, X^*\cap X_1)$ implies this result for $(X, X^*)$, so we may assume that $X$  has pure dimension one. Then $X_{\rm sing}$ is the finite set of singular points of $X$ and $X^*$ is thus any finite set of closed points of $X$  such that $X\setminus X^*$ is regular.  Following Remark~\ref{rem:CH1=Pic}  (going back to \cite[Proposition 1.4]{LW}) we have the isomorphism ${\operatorname{CH}}^1(X,X^*)\cong {\rm Pic}(X)$ sending the class of a 0-cycle  $z=\sum_in_ix_i \in Z^1(X\setminus X^*)$ to the class of the invertible sheaf ${\mathcal O}_X(z)$; in particular, for each invertible sheaf ${\mathcal L}$ on $X$, there is a $z\in Z^1(X\setminus X^*)$ with ${\mathcal L}\cong  {\mathcal O}_X(z)$.  Now, each  $W\subset X\times{\mathbb P}^1$ satisfying properties \eqref{eqn:Properties}(i.-iii.) is a Cartier divisor, giving the invertible sheaf ${\mathcal O}_{X\times{\mathbb P}^1}(W)$, and 
we have isomorphisms
\[
{\mathcal O}_X(W\cdot X\times \{0\})\cong i_0^*{\mathcal O}_{X\times{\mathbb P}^1}(W),\  {\mathcal O}_X(W\cdot X\times \{\infty\})\cong i_\infty^*{\mathcal O}_{X\times{\mathbb P}^1}(W),
\]
where $i_0, i_\infty$ are the closed immersions $X\times\{0\}\hookrightarrow X\times{\mathbb P}^1$, $X\times\{\infty\}\hookrightarrow X\times{\mathbb P}^1$. By the ${\mathbb P}^1$-bundle formula, the projections $p_1:X\times{\mathbb P}^1\to X$, $p_2:X\times{\mathbb P}^1\to {\mathbb P}^1$ induce an isomorphism
\[
{\rm Pic}(X)\times {\rm Pic}({\mathbb P}^1)\xrightarrow{p_1^*\otimes p_2^*}{\rm Pic}(X\times{\mathbb P}^1)
\]
so ${\mathcal O}_X(W)\cong p_1^*{\mathcal O}_X(z)\otimes p_2^*{\mathcal O}_{{\mathbb P}^1}(m)$ for some $z\in Z^1(X\setminus X^*)$, $m\in {\mathbb Z}$. Thus 
\[
[W\cdot X\times \{0\}]=[z]=[W\cdot X\times \{\infty\}]\in {\operatorname{CH}}^1(X, X^*)
\]
so $W\cdot (X\times \{0\}-X\times \{\infty\})$ is in $R^1(X,X^*)$ and thus $\tilde{R}^1(X, X^*)\subset R^1(X, X^*)$.

In case $X$ has pure dimension zero, we have   $R^0(X, X^*)=\tilde{R}^0(X,X^*)=\{0\}$, so Theorem~\ref{thm:Relations} holds for all $X$ of dimension $\le 1$.
<!-- end remark-10 -->
<!-- lemma-5: body_md -->
\label{lem:Bertini} Let $Y\subset {\mathbb P}^N$ be a reduced quasi-projective scheme over an infinite field $k$, and let $\check{{\mathbb P}}^N$ denote the dual projective space of hyperplanes. Then there is a Zariski dense open subset $U\subset \check{{\mathbb P}}^N$ such that for each $H\in U(k)$, the scheme-theoretic intersection $H\cap Y$ is reduced.
<!-- end lemma-5 -->
<!-- remark-11: body_md -->
Given a quasi-projective $k$-scheme $Y$ and coherent sheaves ${\mathcal F}_1,\ldots, {\mathcal F}_m$, when we say that a property $P$ holds for all sufficiently general $(s_1,\ldots, s_m)\in \prod_{i=1}^mH^0(Y, {\mathcal F}_i)$, we mean there is projective closure $j:Y\hookrightarrow \bar{Y}$ of $Y$, coherent sheaves $\bar{{\mathcal F}}_1,\ldots, \bar{{\mathcal F}}_m$ on $\bar{Y}$ with $j^*\bar{{\mathcal F}}_i\cong {\mathcal F}_i$ and a Zariski open subset $U\subset \prod_{i=1}^mH^0(\bar{Y}, \bar{{\mathcal F}}_i)$ (viewing this product as a product of the associated affine spaces) such that $P$ holds for all $(s_1,\ldots, s_m)\in \prod_{i=1}^mH^0(Y, {\mathcal F}_i)$ with $s_i=j^*\bar{s}_i$ and with $(\bar{s}_1,\ldots, \bar{s}_m)\in U(k)$.
<!-- end remark-11 -->
<!-- lemma-6: body_md -->
\label{lem:ClosedImmersion} Let $f:V\to U$ be a finite \'etale morphism in ${\operatorname{\mathbf{Sch}}}_k$ and let $i:Z\to V$ be a closed subscheme of $V$. Let $u\in U$ be a point and let  $\bar{u}:{\rm Spec\,} F\to U$ be geometric point  factoring through $u$. Suppose that the projection $Z\times_U{\rm Spec\,} F\to {\rm Spec\,} F$ is an isomorphism. Then there is a Zariski open neighborhood $U_u$ of $u$ in $U$ such that $Z\times_UU_u\to U_u$ is a closed immersion.
<!-- end lemma-6 -->
<!-- proof-8: body_md -->
We may assume that $F$ is an algebraic closure $\overline{k(u)}$ of $k(u)$. Let ${\mathcal O}^{sh}_{U,u}$ be the strict henselization of the local ring ${\mathcal O}_{U,u}$, giving us the canonical extension of $\bar{u}$ to a morphism  $u^{sh}:{\rm Spec\,}{\mathcal O}^{sh}_{U,u}\to U$ and the  diagram with all squares cartesian
\[
\xymatrix{
Z\times_U{\rm Spec\,} \overline{k(u)}\ar[d]^{\bar{i}}\ar[r]&Z\times_U{\rm Spec\,}{\mathcal O}^{sh}_{U,u}\ar[d]^{i^{sh}}\ar[r]&Z\ar[d]^i\\
V\times_U{\rm Spec\,} \overline{k(u)}\ar[d]^{\bar{f}}\ar[r]&V\times_U{\rm Spec\,}{\mathcal O}^{sh}_{U,u}\ar[d]^{f^{sh}}\ar[r]&V\ar[d]^f\\
{\rm Spec\,} \overline{k(u)}\ar[r]\ar@/_20pt/[rr]_{\bar{u}}&{\rm Spec\,}{\mathcal O}^{sh}_{U,u}\ar[r]^-{u^{sh}}&U
}
\]
Since $f$ is finite (say of degree $d$)  and \'etale, $V\times_U{\rm Spec\,}{\mathcal O}^{sh}_{U,u}$ is isomorphic to a finite disjoint union of $d$ copies of ${\rm Spec\,}{\mathcal O}^{sh}_{U,u}$, with $f^{sh}$ the product of $d$ identity maps
\[
V\times_U{\rm Spec\,}{\mathcal O}^{sh}_{U,u}=\amalg_{i=1}^d{\rm Spec\,}{\mathcal O}^{sh}_{U,u}\xrightarrow{\prod_{i=1}^d{\operatorname{\rm Id}}} {\rm Spec\,}{\mathcal O}^{sh}_{U,u}.
\]
The map $\bar{f}$ breaks up as a disjoint union of identity maps ${\rm Spec\,} \overline{k(u)}\to {\rm Spec\,} \overline{k(u)}$ and the maps $\bar{i}$ and $i^{sh}$ similarly break up into a disjoint union of closed immersions. By assumption, the map $\bar{f}\bar{i}:Z\times_U{\rm Spec\,} \overline{k(u)}\to {\rm Spec\,} \overline{k(u)}$ is an isomorphism, so the map $\bar{i}$ maps $Z\times_U{\rm Spec\,} \overline{k(u)}={\rm Spec\,} \overline{k(u)}$ to a single component in $V\times_U{\rm Spec\,} \overline{k(u)}$; as each component in $V\times_U{\rm Spec\,}{\mathcal O}^{sh}_{U,u}$ is local with closed point $V\times_U{\rm Spec\,} \overline{k(u)}\cong {\rm Spec\,} \overline{k(u)}$, this implies that $i^{sh}:Z\times_U{\rm Spec\,}{\mathcal O}^{sh}_{U,u}\to V\times_U{\rm Spec\,}{\mathcal O}^{sh}_{U,u}$ is a closed immersion of $Z\times_U{\rm Spec\,}{\mathcal O}^{sh}_{U,u}$ into a single component of $V\times_U{\rm Spec\,}{\mathcal O}^{sh}_{U,u}$. Thus $f^{sh}\circ i^{sh}:Z\times_U{\rm Spec\,}{\mathcal O}^{sh}_{U,u}\to {\rm Spec\,}{\mathcal O}^{sh}_{U,u}$ is a closed immersion.

On the other hand, the map $f\circ i:Z\to U$ is a finite morphism. Let ${\mathcal K}$ be the cokernel of the canonical map ${\mathcal O}_U\to  (f\circ i)_*{\mathcal O}_Z$. Then $f\circ i$ is a closed immersion over some open neighborhood $U_u$ of $u$ if and only if  ${\mathcal K}|_{U_u}=0$.  Since $f^{sh}\circ i^{sh}$ is a closed immersion, we have ${\mathcal K}\otimes_{{\mathcal O}_U}{\mathcal O}^{sh}_{U,u}=0$ and since $u^{sh}$ is flat, this implies that ${\mathcal K}\otimes_{{\mathcal O}_U}{\mathcal O}_{U,u}=0$. Since ${\mathcal K}$ is a coherent sheaf, there is thus an open neighborhood $U_u$ of $u$ such that ${\mathcal K}|_{U_u}=0$, and thus $f\circ i$ is a closed immersion over $U_u$.
<!-- end proof-8 -->
<!-- lemma-7: body_md -->
\label{lem:GenPos} Let $(X, X^*)$ be an admissible pair, suppose that $X$ is connected and $d:={\operatorname{\rm dim}}_kX\ge 2$. Let $W\subset X\times {\mathbb P}^1$ be a pure dimension one closed subscheme  satisfying properties \eqref{eqn:Properties}(i.-iii.); we assume in addition that each irreducible component of $W$ has non-empty intersection with $X^*\times{\mathbb P}^1$.   Let $\hat{W}=p_1(W)$.  Fix a (locally closed) projective embedding  $i:X\times{\mathbb P}^1\to {\mathbb P}^N$, with corresponding very ample invertible sheaf ${\mathcal O}_{X\times{\mathbb P}^1}(1)$ on $X\times{\mathbb P}^1$.
Then for  $0\ll m_1\ll m_2\ll\ldots\ll m_d$ sufficiently large, and $g_1,\ldots, g_d\in \prod_iH^0(X\times{\mathbb P}^1, {\mathcal I}_W(m_i))$ sufficiently general, we have 
\begin{equation}\label{eqn:GenPos}
V(g_1,\ldots, g_d)\subset X_{\operatorname{C-M}}\times {\mathbb P}^1\amalg X(d-1)^0\times{\mathbb P}^1.
\end{equation}
Let $H:=V(g_1)\cap X(d)^0\times {\mathbb P}^1$, let  $V(g_1,\ldots, g_d)_H:=V(g_1,\ldots, g_d)\cap H$ and let $E$ be the closure of $V(g_1,\ldots, g_d)_H\setminus W$ in $H$. We  have in addition:\\[5pt]
i.  $H$ and $E$ are both reduced, $H$ is a Cartier divisor on $X(d)^0\times{\mathbb P}^1$. Both  $V(g_1,\ldots, g_d)_H$ and  $E$ are  closed subschemes of  pure codimension $d$ in $X\times {\mathbb P}^1$.\\[2pt]
ii. For each $i=1,\dots, d$, $V(g_1,\ldots, g_i)$ has pure codimension $i$ on $X\times{\mathbb P}^1$, $g_1,\ldots, g_i$ form a regular sequence at each point of $V(g_1,\ldots, g_i)\cap X(d)^0\times {\mathbb P}^1$ and $V(g_1,\ldots, g_d)=W$ in a neighborhood of $W\cap X^*\times{\mathbb P}^1$.\\[2pt]
iii. $E\cap (X^*\times\{0,\infty\})=\0$, $E\cap W\cap  (X^*\times{\mathbb P}^1)=\0$ and $E$ and $W$ have no common components.\\[2pt]
iv. Let $p_1:X\times{\mathbb P}^1\to X$  be the first projection and let $\hat{W}=p_1(W_{\rm red})$. Then we have
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(a)] $p_1:V(g_1)\to X$ is finite. There is an open subscheme $U_1$ of $X(d)^0\setminus \hat{W}$ that contains   each generic point of $X^*\cap X(d)^0\setminus \hat{W}$ and such that $p_1:H\to X(d)^0$ is \'etale over $U_1$.
\item[(b)]   There is an open subscheme $U_2$ of $U_1$,   containing each generic point of $X^*(d-1)$, such that,  for $i=2,\ldots, d$,  $V(g_1,\ldots, g_i)\cap U_2\times{\mathbb P}^1$ is dense in $V(g_1,\ldots, g_i)\cap  X(d)^0\times{\mathbb P}^1\setminus W)$ and  $p_1: V(g_1,\ldots, g_i)\cap (U_2\times{\mathbb P}^1)\to U_2$ is a closed immersion.
\end{enumerate}
v.  $E\cap (X^*\times{\mathbb P}^1)\subset U_2\times{\mathbb P}^1$.\\[2pt]
vi. $E$ is a local complete intersection in $H$ in a neighborhood of $E\cap (X^*\times{\mathbb P}^1)$.\\[2pt]
vii. Let $C:=V(g_1,\ldots, g_d)_H$. Then $C$ is a local complete intersection in $H$, and we have the identity of 0-cycles on $X\times\{0,\infty\}$.
\[
[|C|\cdot (X\times\{0,\infty\})]=[|W|\cdot(X\times\{0,\infty\})]+[|E|\cdot (X\times\{0,\infty\})]\\
\]
<!-- end lemma-7 -->
<!-- proof-9: body_md -->
This closely follows the proof of \cite[Lemma 3]{BS98}. 

It follows from property \eqref{eqn:Properties}(i) that $W\subset X_{\operatorname{C-M}}\times{\mathbb P}^1\subset X(d)^0\times{\mathbb P}^1$; since each irreducible component of $W$ intersects $X^*\times{\mathbb P}^1$ in a finite set, $W$ contains no fibers $\{x\}\times{\mathbb P}^1$, $x\in X$. Also, $\hat{W}\subset X_{\operatorname{C-M}}$ and $\hat{W}\cap X^*$ is finite.
 
 
 
 As in the proof of Lemma~\ref{lem:MovingLemmaR0}, we can assume that  $V(g_1,\ldots, g_d)\cap U=W\cap U$ for some neighborhood $U$ of $W\cap X^*\times{\mathbb P}^1$ in $X_{\operatorname{C-M}}\times{\mathbb P}^1$ (depending on $g_1,\ldots, g_d$), and $V(g_1,\ldots, g_d)\cap T=\0$ for $T$ a  given closed subset of $X\times{\mathbb P}^1\setminus U$ of dimension $\le d-1$.  As 
 \[
 {\operatorname{\rm dim}}_k(X\setminus (X_{\operatorname{C-M}}\times{\mathbb P}^1\amalg X(d-1)^0\times{\mathbb P}^1))\le d-1
 \]
 this  proves \eqref{eqn:GenPos}.

Let $\{x_1,\ldots, x_t\}=W_{\rm red}\cap X^*\times{\mathbb P}^1$. At each $x_i$,   ${\mathcal I}_{W,x_i}/{\mathcal I}_{W,x_i}^2$ is a $k(x_i)$-vector space of dimension $d$. 

For (i), consider the blow-up $\mu:(X\times{\mathbb P}^1)_W\to X\times{\mathbb P}^1$ with exceptional (Cartier) divisor $D$. The invertible sheaf ${\mathcal O}_{(X\times{\mathbb P}^1)_W}(-D)$ is relatively very ample, so  $\mu^*{\mathcal O}_{X\times{\mathbb P}^1}(m_1)(-D)$ is very ample on $(X\times{\mathbb P}^1)_W$ for $m_1\gg0$. We take a corresponding locally closed embedding $(X\times{\mathbb P}^1)_W\subset {\mathbb P}^M$ with ${\mathcal O}_{(X\times{\mathbb P}^1)_W}(1)=\mu^*{\mathcal O}_{X\times{\mathbb P}^1}(m_1)(-D)$.

Moreover, since $W$ is a complete intersection in a neighborhood of each $x_i$, the map $D\to W$ is a ${\mathbb P}^{d-1}$-bundle over a neighborhood of each $x_i$, with fibers embedded as linear subspaces of ${\mathbb P}^M$. Letting $D_{x_i}\cong {\mathbb P}^{d-1}$ denote the fiber over $x_i$, we have
\[
\mu^*{\mathcal O}_{X\times{\mathbb P}^1}(m_1)(-D)\otimes {\mathcal O}_{D_{x_i}}\cong {\mathcal O}_{{\mathbb P}^{d-1}}(1)
\]
and the restriction map 
\[
H^0({\mathbb P}^M, {\mathcal O}_{{\mathbb P}^M}(1))\to H^0(D_{x_i}, {\mathcal O}_{D_{x_i}}(1))
\]
is surjective (we trivialize ${\mathcal O}_{X\times{\mathbb P}^1}(m_1)$ in a neighborhood of $x_i$ to avoid writing the twist). Identifying $H^0(D_{x_i}, {\mathcal O}_{D_{x_i}}(1))$ with ${\mathcal I}_{W,x_i}/{\mathcal I}_{W,x_i}^2\otimes_{{\mathcal O}_W}k(x_i)$,  and recalling that 
\[
\mu_*(\mu^*{\mathcal O}_{X\times{\mathbb P}^1}(m_1)(-D))={\mathcal I}_W(m_1)
\]
we see that there is a dense open subset $\tilde{V}$ of $H^0({\mathbb P}^M, {\mathcal O}_{{\mathbb P}^M}(1))$ such that for $y\in\tilde{V}(k)$, the  corresponding global section $g_y$ of  ${\mathcal I}_W(m_1)$ restricts to a non-zero element of ${\mathcal I}_{W,x_i}/{\mathcal I}_{W,x_i}^2\otimes_{{\mathcal O}_W}k(x_i)$ for each $i=1,\ldots, r$.

In what follows, for $s_1,\ldots, s_j\in H^0({\mathbb P}^N, {\mathcal O}_{{\mathbb P}^N}(m))$, we write $V(s_1,\ldots, s_j)$ for the closed subscheme of $X\times{\mathbb P}^1$ defined by the restrictions of the $s_i$; similarly, for sections  $s_1,\ldots, s_j\in H^0({\mathbb P}^M, {\mathcal O}_{{\mathbb P}^M}(r))$, we have $V(s_1,\ldots, s_j)\subset (X\times{\mathbb P}^1)_W$.

 Note that $(X(d)^0\times{\mathbb P}^1)_W\subset (X\times{\mathbb P}^1)_W$ is reduced (see \cite[\href{https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/0808}{Tag 0808}]{stacks-project}).    By the Bertini theorem (Lemma~\ref{lem:Bertini}), there is  a dense open subset of $H^0({\mathbb P}^M, {\mathcal O}_{{\mathbb P}^M}(1))$ whose $k$-points $y$ give sections $\tilde{g}_y$ of $(\mu^*{\mathcal O}_{X\times{\mathbb P}^1}(m_1))(-D)$ such that $V(\tilde{g}_y)\cap (X(d)^0\times{\mathbb P}^1)_W$ is reduced. By the above, we may take $y$ so that the corresponding global section $g_1:=g_y$ of  ${\mathcal I}_W(m_1)$ also restricts to a non-zero element of ${\mathcal I}_{W,x_i}/{\mathcal I}_{W,x_i}^2\otimes_{{\mathcal O}_W}k(x_i)$ for each $x_i$. By our assumption on $W$, we see that $X(d)^0\times{\mathbb P}^1$ is Cohen-Macaulay in a neighborhood of each $x_i$, and hence by unmixedness, $V(g_1)\cap X(d)^0\times{\mathbb P}^1$ is reduced outside of a closed subset $W_0$ of $W$ contained in $W\setminus X^*\times{\mathbb P}^1$. Since $W$ has dimension one,  and each irreducible component of $W$ intersects $X^*\times{\mathbb P}^1$, $W_0$ is a finite set of points of $(X(d)^0\setminus X^*)\times{\mathbb P}^1\subset X_{\operatorname{reg}}(d)\times{\mathbb P}^1$. Thus, for each $x\in W_0$,   ${\mathcal O}_{X\times{\mathbb P}^1,x}$ is a regular local ring of dimension $d+1$, hence Cohen-Macaulay of dimension $>2$, so $V(g_1)$ is reduced at $x\in W_0$ as well. Thus taking $H=V(g_1)\cap X(d)^0\times{\mathbb P}^1$, $H$ is thus a reduced Cartier divisor on $X(d)^0\times{\mathbb P}^1$.
 
We have $(W\cap X^*\times{\mathbb P}^1)\cup (X\setminus X^*)\times{\mathbb P}^1\subset X_{\operatorname{C-M}}\times{\mathbb P}^1$ As mentioned in Remarks~\ref{rem:Prelims}, $X_{\operatorname{C-M}}$ is an open subset of $X(d)^0$ and of $X$, and  the complement of $X_{\operatorname{C-M}}$ in $X(d)$ has codimension at least two. 

Let $H_{\operatorname{C-M}}$ be the Cohen-Macaulay locus in $H$. Since $g_1$ is a non-zero divisor on $X(d)^0\times{\mathbb P}^1$, we have
\[
H_{\operatorname{C-M}}\supset  H\cap X_{\operatorname{C-M}}\times{\mathbb P}^1\supset (W\cap X^*\times{\mathbb P}^1)\cup (H\cap (X\setminus X^*)\times{\mathbb P}^1).
\]

Let  $\overline{X\times{\mathbb P}^1}$ and $\bar{W}\subset \overline{X\times{\mathbb P}^1}$  be the closures of $X\times{\mathbb P}^1$ and $W$ in ${\mathbb P}^N$, and let ${\mathcal I}_{\bar{W}}\subset {\mathcal O}_{\overline{X\times{\mathbb P}^1}}$ be the ideal sheaf.  It follows by an easy induction that for $m_1\ll m_2\ll\ldots\ll m_d$, there is a dense open subset 
\[
U\subset \prod_{j=1}^dH^0(\overline{X\times{\mathbb P}^1}, {\mathcal I}_{\bar{W}}(m_1))\times\ldots\times H^0(\overline{X\times{\mathbb P}^1}, {\mathcal I}_{\bar{W}}(m_d))
\]
such that, for $(g_1,\ldots, g_d)\in U(k)$, we have:\\[5pt]
a. \eqref{eqn:GenPos} holds.\\[2pt]
b. For each $i=1,\ldots, d$,  $g_1,\ldots, g_i$ restricts to a regular sequence on $X(d)^0\times{\mathbb P}^1$, $V(g_1,\ldots, g_i)\cap X(d)^0\times{\mathbb P}^1$ is a reduced closed subscheme of $X(d)^0\times{\mathbb P}^1$, of pure codimension $i$, and $V(g_1,\ldots, g_i)\cap(X_{\operatorname{C-M}} \times{\mathbb P}^1)$ is Cohen-Macaulay.  \\[2pt]
c.  $g_1,\ldots, g_d$ generate ${\mathcal I}_{W, x}$ at each point $x\in W\cap X^*\times{\mathbb P}^1$.\\[2pt]
\\[2pt]
By \eqref{eqn:GenPos} the closed subscheme $V(g_1,\ldots, g_d)$ of $X\times{\mathbb P}^1$ is a disjoint union of two closed subschemes $V(g_1,\ldots, g_d)_H\subset X_{\operatorname{C-M}}\times{\mathbb P}^1$ and $V(g_1,\ldots, g_d)\cap (X(d-1)^0\times{\mathbb P}^1)$, hence   $V(g_1,\ldots, g_d)_H$ is also closed in $X\times{\mathbb P}^1$. Since $E$ is closed in $V(g_1,\ldots, g_d)_H$, this implies that $E$ is also closed in $X\times{\mathbb P}^1$. Together with (a)-(c), this  implies (i) and (ii). 

In addition, by (c), there is an open neighborhood $V$ of $W\cap X^*\times{\mathbb P}^1$ in $X\times{\mathbb P}^1$ such that $V(g_1,\ldots, g_d)\cap V=W\cap V$. This shows that $E\cap W\cap X^*\times{\mathbb P}^1=\0$. If we now consider $X^*\times\{0,\infty\}$, since $W\cap X^*\times\{0,\infty\}=\0$, we may assume that 
\[
{\rm codim}_{X^*\times\{0,\infty\}}H\cap X^*\times\{0,\infty\}\ge 1
\]
and then by induction on $i$, that 
\begin{equation}\label{eqn:CodimXsing}
\vbox{
${\rm codim}_{X^*\times\{0,\infty\}}V(g_1,\ldots, g_i)\cap X^*\times\{0,\infty\}\ge i$ for all $i=1,\ldots, d$.
}
\end{equation}
 Taking $i=d$, and noting that ${\operatorname{\rm dim}} X^*\le d-1$, we see that $V(g_1,\ldots, g_d)\cap X^*\times\{0,\infty\}=\0$. Since $E\cap W\cap X^*=\0$ and each component of $W$ intersects $X^*\times{\mathbb P}^1$, we see that $E$ and $W$ have no common components,  and we have proven (iii).

For (iv)(a), consider the curves $\{x\}\times{\mathbb P}^1\subset \overline{X\times{\mathbb P}^1}$, $x\in X$. Since $X$ is connected, there is an integer $r\ge1$ such that, for all $x\in X$,  ${\mathcal O}_{\overline{X\times{\mathbb P}^1}}(1)$ restricted to $\{x\}\times{\mathbb P}^1={\mathbb P}^1_x$ is isomorphic to ${\mathcal O}_{{\mathbb P}^1_x}(r)$, that is, the curves $\{x\}\times{\mathbb P}^1$ are all curves of degree $r$ in ${\mathbb P}^N$. 

There is an integer $m_0>0$ such that  for all $x\in X$, and all $m\ge m_0$ the restriction map
\[
H^0(\overline{X\times{\mathbb P}^1}, {\mathcal I}_{\bar{W}}(m))\to H^0(\{x\}\times{\mathbb P}^1, {\mathcal I}_W\otimes_{{\mathcal O}_{X\times{\mathbb P}^1}}{\mathcal O}_{\{x\}\times{\mathbb P}^1}(rm))
\]
is  surjective, and $H^1(\{x\}\times{\mathbb P}^1, {\mathcal I}_W\otimes_{{\mathcal O}_{X\times{\mathbb P}^1}}{\mathcal O}_{\{x\}\times{\mathbb P}^1}(rm))=0$. Choosing a section $s\in H^0(\{x\}\times{\mathbb P}^1, {\mathcal O}_{\{x\}\times{\mathbb P}^1}(r))$ with $V(s)\cap W=\0$, we have the exact sequence
\[
0\to {\mathcal I}_W\otimes_{{\mathcal O}_{X\times{\mathbb P}^1}}{\mathcal O}_{\{x\}\times{\mathbb P}^1}(rm)\xrightarrow{\times s}
{\mathcal I}_W\otimes_{{\mathcal O}_{X\times{\mathbb P}^1}}{\mathcal O}_{\{x\}\times{\mathbb P}^1}(r(m+1))\to 
{\mathcal O}_{V(s)}\to 0, 
\]
giving 
\begin{multline*}
{\operatorname{\rm dim}}_kH^0(\{x\}\times{\mathbb P}^1, {\mathcal I}_W\otimes_{X\times{\mathbb P}^1}{\mathcal O}_{\{x\}\times{\mathbb P}^1}(rm))\\=
H^0(\{x\}\times{\mathbb P}^1, {\mathcal I}_W\otimes_{{\mathcal O}_{X\times{\mathbb P}^1}}{\mathcal O}_{\{x\}\times{\mathbb P}^1}(rm_0))+(m-m_0)r
\end{multline*}
for all $m\ge m_0$. In particular, for all integers $m_1> m_0+{\operatorname{\rm dim}}_kX/r$, we have
\[
{\operatorname{\rm dim}}_kH^0(\{x\}\times{\mathbb P}^1, {\mathcal I}_W\otimes_{X\times{\mathbb P}^1}{\mathcal O}_{\{x\}\times{\mathbb P}^1}(rm_1))>{\operatorname{\rm dim}}_kX
\]
We have the constructible subset
\[
F_0^0:=\{g\in H^0(\overline{X\times{\mathbb P}^1}, {\mathcal I}_{\bar{W}}(m_1))\setminus\{0\}\mid \exists x\in X\text{ with } V(g)\supset \{x\}\times{\mathbb P}^1\}
\]
of $H^0(\overline{X\times{\mathbb P}^1}, {\mathcal I}_{\bar{W}}(m_1))$. By the theorem on the dimension of fibers \cite[\S 6.3, Theorem 1.25]{Shafarevich}, the closure $F_0$ of $F^0_0$
has codimension at least one in $H^0(\overline{X\times{\mathbb P}^1}, {\mathcal I}_{\bar{W}}(m_1))$. This gives us the dense open subset
\[
V_0= H^0(\overline{X\times{\mathbb P}^1}, {\mathcal I}_{\bar{W}}(m_1))\setminus F_0\subset H^0(\overline{X\times{\mathbb P}^1}, {\mathcal I}_{\bar{W}}(m_1)), 
\]
such that,  for all $g\in V_0(k)$, the projection $p_1:V(g)\to X$ is quasi-finite and proper, hence finite. This proves the first assertion in (iv)(a).

For the rest of (iv)(a),  if we take $x\in X\setminus \hat{W}$, then ${\mathcal I}_W\otimes{\mathcal O}_{\{x\}\times{\mathbb P}^1}(m_1)={\mathcal O}_{\{x\}\times{\mathbb P}^1}(m_1)$,  and the restriction map
\[
H^0(\overline{X\times{\mathbb P}^1}, {\mathcal I}_{\bar{W}}(m_1))\to H^0(\{x\}\times {\mathbb P}^1, {\mathcal O}_{\{x\}\times{\mathbb P}^1}(rm_1))
\] 
is surjective. For each irreducible component $X^*_i$ of $X^*\cap X(d)^0\setminus \hat{W}$, choose a closed point $x_i\in X^*_i\setminus W$, not lying in $X^*_j$ for each $j\neq i$. Increasing $m_1$ if necessary, the restriction map
\[
H^0(\overline{X\times{\mathbb P}^1}, {\mathcal I}_{\bar{W}}(m_1))\to \oplus_i H^0(\{x_i\}\times {\mathbb P}^1, {\mathcal O}_{{\mathbb P}^1_x}(rm_1))
\] 
is still surjective.


Let $X_0, X_1$ be  the standard coordinates on ${\mathbb P}^1$, identifying $H^0({\mathbb P}^1_x, {\mathcal O}_{{\mathbb P}^1_x}(rm_1))$ with homogeneous polynomials of degree $m_1r$ in $X_0, X_1$.  Then the subset of $H^0({\mathbb P}^1_x, {\mathcal O}_{{\mathbb P}^1_x}(rm_1))$ consisting of polynomials $f(X_0, X_1)$ with $m_1r$ distinct roots (in a suitable algebraic closure) is open and dense. Choose for each irreducible component $X^*_j$ of $X^*\cap X(d)^0\setminus \hat{W}$ a closed point $y_j\in X_j^*\cap X(d)^0\setminus \hat{W}$.  Then there is a dense open subset $V$ of $H^0(\overline{X\times{\mathbb P}^1}, {\mathcal I}_{\bar{W}}(m_1))$ such that, for each $g_1\in V(k)$, $V(g_1)\cap X(d)^0\times{\mathbb P}^1$ is reduced  Cartier divisor on $X(d)^0\times{\mathbb P}^1$, $p_1:V(g_1)\to X$ is finite and the restriction of $g_1$ to $\{y_j\}\times{\mathbb P}^1$ has $m_1r$ distinct roots for each $y_j$. This implies that $p_1:V(g_1)\to X$ is \'etale over an open subscheme $U_1$ of $X(d)^0$ containing each $y_j$, hence containing each generic point of $X^*\cap X(d)^0\setminus \hat{W}$.  Since $H=V(g_1)\cap X(d)^0\times{\mathbb P}^1$, this completes the proof of (iv)(a).


For (iv)(b), we may remove from $X$ any closed subset $T$ such that $T\cap W\cap X^*=\0$ and $T$ contains no component of $X^*(d-1)$. In particular, we   may assume that $X=X(d)=X(d)^0$ and $X^*=X^*(d-1)$. Since $d\ge2$, $X^*$ has no zero-dimensional components, and no generic point of $X^*$ is in $W$. We may further assume that $X=X_{\operatorname{C-M}}$ and $X\setminus W=U_1$. Taking $(g_1,\ldots, g_d)$ as above, we have $H=V(g_1)$,   $H\subset X\times{\mathbb P}^1$ is finite over $X$, and  $H$ is \'etale over $U_1=X\setminus W$.

It suffices to prove the case $i=2$. Indeed, assuming the case $i=2$,  and given $i$, $2<i\le d$, $V(g_1,\ldots, g_i)\cap U_2\times {\mathbb P}^1$ is a closed subscheme of $V(g_1, g_2)\cap U_2\times{\mathbb P}^1$, so $p_1:V(g_1,\ldots, g_i)\cap U_2\times {\mathbb P}^1\to U_2$ is still a closed immersion. As the base-locus of $H^0(\overline{X\times{\mathbb P}^1}, {\mathcal I}_{\bar{W}}(m_j))$ is $\bar{W}$ (for all $m_j$ sufficiently large),  we need only take $g_3,\ldots, g_i$ sufficiently general so that   $V(g_1,\ldots, g_i)\cap X\times {\mathbb P}^1\setminus W$ intersects each component of $(X\setminus U_2)\times{\mathbb P}^1\setminus W$ properly, and (iv)(b) is satisfied. 

For the case $i=2$, take $m_2\gg m_1$, chosen so that the restriction map  
\begin{equation}\label{eqn:ResSurjectivity}
H^0(\overline{X\times{\mathbb P}^1}, {\mathcal I}_W(m_2))\to H^0(\{u\}\times{\mathbb P}^1, {\mathcal O}_{\{u\}\times{\mathbb P}^1}(m_2r))
\end{equation}
is surjective for all $u\in U_1$. 

Let $M={\operatorname{\rm dim}}_kH^0(\overline{X\times{\mathbb P}^1}, {\mathcal I}_{\bar{W}}(m_2))-1$, giving us the corresponding linear system ${\mathbb P}^M$ of divisors  on $\overline{X\times{\mathbb P}^1}$. Inside ${\mathbb P}^M$ we have the dense open subset ${\mathbb P}^M_0$ consisting of points $[D]$ such that the corresponding divisor $D$  does not contain any fiber $\{x\}\times{\mathbb P}^1$, $x\in X$. Let $I\subset \overline{X\times{\mathbb P}^1}\times {\mathbb P}^M$ be the incidence correspondence, and let $I'=I\cap (U_1\times {\mathbb P}^1\cap H)\times{\mathbb P}^M_0\subset U_1\times{\mathbb P}^1\times{\mathbb P}^M_0$. Since $H\to X(d)^0$ is finite, the map $p_{13}:I'\to U_1\times{\mathbb P}^M_0$ is finite, giving us the reduced closed subscheme $P:=p_{13}(I')\subset U_1\times{\mathbb P}^M_0$, with geometric points
\[
\{(u, [D])\in U_1\times {\mathbb P}^M_0\mid D\cap H\cap \{u\}\times{\mathbb P}^1\neq\0\}.
\]
Let $P'\subset P$ be the subset  with geometric points
\[
\{(u, [D])\mid \deg_{k(u)}(D\cap H\cap \{u\}\times{\mathbb P}^1)\ge 2\};
\]
the upper-semi-continuity of dimension for the proper pushforward of coherent sheaves \cite[Theorem 12.8]{Hartshorne} implies that $P'$ is a closed subset of $P$. We consider $P'$ as a reduced closed subscheme of $P$. For  $T\subset U_1$ a locally closed subscheme, let $P(T)=(P\cap T\times{\mathbb P}^M_0)_{\rm red}$, $P'(T)=(P'\cap T\times{\mathbb P}^M_0)_{\rm red}$. Since $H\to X(d)^0$ is finite and \'etale of degree $m_1r$ over $U_1$, the surjectivity of \eqref{eqn:ResSurjectivity} tell us that, for each $u\in U_1$, $P(u)$ is the union of $m_1r$ distinct codimension one linear subspaces of ${\mathbb P}^M_{\overline{k(u)}}$, intersected with ${\mathbb P}^M_{0, k(u)}$, and $P'(u)\subset P(u)$ is a similar union of codimension two linear subspaces of ${\mathbb P}^M_{\overline{k(u)}}$, intersected with ${\mathbb P}^M_{0, k(u)}$. Thus ${\operatorname{\rm dim}}_{k(u)}P(u)=M-1$ or $P(u)=\0$, and ${\operatorname{\rm dim}}_{k(u)}P'(u)=M-2$ or $P'(u)=\0$. 

We apply the theorem on the dimension of fibers  \cite[\S 6.3, Theorem 1.25]{Shafarevich} to the projection to $U_1$, which tells us that, for $T\subset U_1$ an closed subset of pure dimension $e$,  $P(T)$ has dimension $e+M-1$ (or is empty), and  $P'(T)$ has dimension $e+M-2$ (or is empty). Taking the projection to ${\mathbb P}^M_0$, this implies there is a dense open subscheme $V_T\subset {\mathbb P}^M_0$ such that the projection $P(T)\to {\mathbb P}^M_0$ has fiber dimension  $e-1$ over $V_T$ (or has all fibers  over $V_T$ empty), and $P'(T)\to {\mathbb P}^M_0$ has fiber dimension  $e-2$ over $V_T$ (or has all fibers  over $V_T$ empty). 

We apply this to $T$ an irreducible component of $X^*\cap U_1$.  We choose $g_2\in H^0(\overline{X\times{\mathbb P}^1}, {\mathcal I}_{\bar{W}}(m_2))\setminus\{0\}$ so that  $[V(g_2)]\in {\mathbb P}^M$ is in $V_T\subset {\mathbb P}^M_0$. Let $Z=V(g_1, g_2)\subset X\times{\mathbb P}^1$, and let $\bar{Z}$ be the image of $Z$ in $X$. Suppose $\bar{Z}\cap T$ is not empty. Since $T$ has dimension $d-1$,  it follows that $Z \cap T\times{\mathbb P}^1$ and $\bar{Z}\cap T$ both have pure dimension $d-2$, and there is a  closed subset $T'$ of $\bar{Z}\cap T$ of dimension $\le d-3$ such that $\bar{u}\times{\mathbb P}^1\cap Z$ is a single point  for each geometric point $\bar{u}\to \bar{Z}\setminus T'$. Since $V(g_1)\to X$ is \'etale and finite over $U_1$, we map apply Lemma~\ref{lem:ClosedImmersion} to find an open subset $U_T$ of $U_1$ with $U_T\cap T=T\setminus T'$, such that $V(g_1, g_2)\to X$ is a closed immersion over $U_T$. Taking $U_2$ to be the union of the $U_T$ over the irreducible components of $X^*\cap U_1$ proves (iv)(b).
 
 For (v), let $F=(X^*\setminus \hat{W})\setminus U_1$, so by (iv)(a), $F$ contains no generic point of $X^*$, in particular each component of $F$ has dimension $\le d-2$. Letting $F_1=F\cup (X^*\cap \hat{W})$,    $F_1\times{\mathbb P}^1$ contains $W\cap X^*\times{\mathbb P}^1$ and each component of $F_1$ has dimension $\le d-2$. Taking the $m_i$ sufficiently large, we may assume that the base-locus of the linear system associated to $H^0(\overline{X\times{\mathbb P}^1}, {\mathcal I}_{\bar{W}}(m_i))$ is exactly $\bar{W}$, so by taking $g_1,\ldots, g_d$ sufficiently general, we have that
 \[
 {\rm codim}_{F_1\times {\mathbb P}^1\setminus W}(V(g_1,\ldots, g_i)\cap (F_1\times {\mathbb P}^1\setminus W))\ge i
 \]
 for $i=1,\ldots, d$, hence
 \[
 (V(g_1,\ldots, g_d)\setminus W)\cap F_1\times {\mathbb P}^1=\0.
 \]
 As $V(g_1,\ldots, g_d)\setminus W=E\setminus E\cap W$ and  $E\cap W\cap X^*\times{\mathbb P}^1=\0$ by (iii), we see that
 \[
 E\cap X^*\times{\mathbb P}^1\subset U_1\times{\mathbb P}^1,
 \]
hence $p_1:H\to X$ is \'etale at each point of $E\cap X^*\times{\mathbb P}^1$. 

Similarly, let $F_2=X^*\cap X(d)^0\setminus U_2$. Then since $U_2 \cap X^*(d-1)$ is dense in $X^*(d-1)$, we see that each component of $F_2$ has dimension $\le d-2$, and thus $E\cap X^*\times{\mathbb P}^1\subset U_2\times{\mathbb P}^1$ for all $g_1,\ldots, g_d$ sufficiently general.

The assertion (vi) follows from (ii), (iii) and the fact that $V(g_1,\ldots, g_d)_H=W\amalg E$ in a neighborhood of $X^*\times {\mathbb P}^1$. To show (vii), we have $V(g_1,\ldots, g_d)_H=W\cup E$ (up to possible 0-dimensional embedded components) and $W$ and $E$ have no common irreducible components, which
 implies the identity of associated cycles
\[
|C|=|W|+|E|.
\]
Since the intersection 0-cycle of $C$, resp. $W$, resp. $E$ with the Cartier divisor $X\times0-X\times\infty$ on $X\times{\mathbb P}^1$ only depends on $|C|$, resp. $|W|$, resp. $|E|$, (vii) follows.
<!-- end proof-9 -->
<!-- proof-10: body_md -->
We may assume that $X$ is connected, and by Remark~\ref{rem:CaseDim1}, we may assume that $X$ has dimension $d\ge2$. 


Let $W\subset X\times{\mathbb P}^1$ be one of the generating curves for $\tilde{R}^d(X,X^*)$. Let $W''$ be the union of the irreducible components of $W$ that have empty intersection with $X_{\rm sing}\times{\mathbb P}^1$, and $W'$ those with non-empty intersection. Let $\hat{W}''=p_1(W'')$, and let
\[
t:={\operatorname{Nm}}_{W''/\hat{W}''}(X_1/X_0)
\]
where $X_0, X_1$ are the standard homogeneous coordinates on ${\mathbb P}^1$, with ${\operatorname{div}}(X_1/X_0)=0-\infty$. Standard arguments (see, e.g., \cite[Proposition 1.4]{Fulton}) show that
\[
{\operatorname{div}}(t)=p_{1*}(|W''|\cdot (X\times\{0\}-X\times\{\infty\}))
\]
and since $\hat{W}''\cap X^*=\0$, we see that 
$p_{1*}(|W''|\cdot (X\times\{0\}-X\times\{\infty\}))$ is in $R^d(X,X^*)$. Thus we may assume from the start that each irreducible component of $W$ intersects $X^*\times{\mathbb P}^1$, putting us in the setting covered by Lemma~\ref{lem:GenPos}; We retain the notations used in the proof of that lemma.

Take $0\ll m_1\ll\ldots\ll m_d$ and $g_i\in H^0(X\times{\mathbb P}^1, {\mathcal I}_W(m_i))$, to satisfy the conclusions of Lemma~\ref{lem:GenPos}; in particular, we have the reduced closed curve $E\subset X\times{\mathbb P}^1$, supported in $X_{\operatorname{C-M}}\times{\mathbb P}^1$, with $V(g_1,\ldots, g_d)_H=E\cup W$ (up to 0-dimensional embedded components). Since the linear systems defined by $H^0(X\times{\mathbb P}^1, {\mathcal I}_W(m_i))$
are base-point free on $X\times{\mathbb P}^1\setminus W$, and $W\subset X_{\operatorname{C-M}}\times{\mathbb P}^1$,  we may assume in addition that\\[5pt]
a. $V(g_1,\ldots, g_{d-1})\cap X\times\{0,\infty\}$ is a disjoint union of  closed subschemes
\[
V(g_1,\ldots, g_{d-1})\cap X\times\{0,\infty\}=E_0\amalg E_\infty\amalg E^*
\]
with $E_0$ a local complete intersection supported in $X_{\operatorname{C-M}}\times\{0\}$, $E_\infty$ a local complete intersection supported in $X_{\operatorname{C-M}}\times\{\infty\}$ and $E^*$ supported in a finite set contained in $X(d-1)^0\times \{0,\infty\}$.   \\[2pt]
b. $V(g_1,\ldots, g_{d-1})\cap X^*\times\{0,\infty\}$ is a finite set of points\\[5pt]
Taking $g_d'$ to be a sufficiently general element of $H^0(X\times{\mathbb P}^1, {\mathcal O}_{X\times{\mathbb P}^1}(m_d))$, by the same arguments we may assume that\\[5pt]
c. $V(g_1,\ldots, g_{d-1}, g_d')$ is a disjoint union of closed subschemes 
\[
V(g_1,\ldots, g_{d-1}, g_d')=V(g_1,\ldots, g_{d-1}, g_d')_{\operatorname{C-M}}\amalg V(g_1,\ldots, g_{d-1}, g_d')_{d-1}
\]
with $V(g_1,\ldots, g_{d-1}, g_d')_{\operatorname{C-M}}$ a local complete intersection supported in $X_{\operatorname{C-M}}\times{\mathbb P}^1$ and $V(g_1,\ldots, g_{d-1}, g_d')_{d-1}$ supported in a finite subset of $X(d-1)^0\times{\mathbb P}^1$.\\[2pt]
d. $V(g_1,\ldots, g_{d-1}, g_d')_{\operatorname{C-M}}\cap X^*\times{\mathbb P}^1$ is a finite set of points.\\[2pt]
e. $V(g_1,\ldots, g_{d-1}, g_d')_{\operatorname{C-M}}\cap X\times\{0,\infty\}$ is supported in $(X\setminus X^*)\times\{0,\infty\}$ and is finite over $k$.\\[5pt]
In addition:\\[5pt]
f. If $d=2$,  then $p_1:V(g_1,\ g_2')\to X(2)^0$ is a closed immersion over some open neighborhood of $p_1(V(g_1, g_2'))\cap X^*\cap X(2)^0$. \\[5pt]
The proof of (f) follows from the same argument used to show that $p_1:V(g_1, g_2)\to X$ is a closed immersion over the open subset $U_2$ given in Lemma~\ref{lem:GenPos}, where the only difference is that $g_2$ was a sufficiently general section of $H^0(X\times{\mathbb P}^1, {\mathcal I}_W(m_2))$ rather than one of $H^0(X\times{\mathbb P}^1, {\mathcal O}_{X\times{\mathbb P}^1}(m_2))$.  

As is standard, for a finite morphism $t:C\to {\mathbb P}^1$, we set ${\operatorname{div}}_0(t)=t^*(0)$, ${\operatorname{div}}_\infty(t)=t^*(\infty)$ and ${\operatorname{div}}(t)={\operatorname{div}}_0(t)-{\operatorname{div}}_\infty(t)$. 

Let $E':=V(g_1,\ldots, g_{d-1}, g_d')_{\operatorname{C-M}}$. Let $\hat{E}'=p_1(E')$ and let $f'={\operatorname{Nm}}_{E'/\hat{E}'}(X_1/X_0)$. 

By Lemma~\ref{lem:GenPos},  $p_1:E'\to \hat{E}'$ is an isomorphism over a neighborhood of $\hat{E}'\cap X^*$, so it follows from (a)-(f)  that $\hat{E}'\cap X^*$ is a finite set of points, all contained in $X_{\operatorname{C-M}}$, $\hat{E}'$ is a complete intersection  on $X$ in a neighborhood of $\hat{E}'\cap X^*$, and $f'$ is in ${\mathcal O}_{\hat{E}': \hat{E}'\cap X^*}^\times$. Thus  $\hat{E}'$ is a Cartier curve on $X$ relative to $X^*$, and we have the element $i_{\hat{E}'*}({\operatorname{div}} f')\in R^d(X, X^*)$.


The curve $E_0$ is supported in $X(d)=X(d)\times\{0\}$, satisfies the conditions of Definition~\ref{def:CartierCurve}, and has empty intersection with $X(\le d-1)$, hence $E_0$ is a Cartier curve on $X$ relative to $X^*$. Let $f_0$ be the restriction of $g_d/g_d'$ to $E_0$. Then $f_0$ is in ${\mathcal O}_{E_0: E_0\cap X^*}^\times$, giving the element $i_{E_0*}({\operatorname{div}} f_0)\in R^d(X, X^*)$.
Similarly,  $E_\infty$ is a Cartier on $X$ relative to $X^*$, and  letting $f_\infty$ be the restriction of $g_d/g_d'$ to $E_\infty$, $f_\infty$ is in ${\mathcal O}_{E_\infty: E_\infty\cap X^*}^\times$ and we have the element $i_{E_\infty*}({\operatorname{div}} f_\infty)\in R^d(X, X^*)$.

Let $\hat{E}=p_1(E)\subset X_{\operatorname{C-M}}$ and let $f={\operatorname{Nm}}_{E/\hat{E}}(X_1/X_0)$. By Lemma~\ref{lem:GenPos} again,  $\hat{E}$ is a Cartier curve on $X$ relative to $X^*$, and $f$ is in ${\mathcal O}_{\hat{E}: \hat{E}\cap X^*}^\times$, so we have the element $i_{\hat{E}*}({\operatorname{div}} f)\in R^d(X, X^*)$.


Finally, we have
\begin{align*}
&(|W|+|E|)\cdot X\times\{0\}=i_{E_0*}({\operatorname{div}}_0(f_0))\\
&(|W|+|E|)\cdot X\times\{\infty\}=i_{E_\infty*}({\operatorname{div}}_0(f_\infty))\\
&|E'|\cdot X\times\{0\}=i_{E_0*}({\operatorname{div}}_\infty(f_0))\\
&|E'|\cdot X\times\{\infty\}=i_{E_\infty*}({\operatorname{div}}_\infty(f_\infty))\\
&i_{\hat{E}'*}({\operatorname{div}} f')=p_{1*}(|E'|\cdot (X\times\{0\}-X\times\{\infty\}))\\
&i_{\hat{E}*}({\operatorname{div}} f)=p_{1*}(|E|\cdot (X\times\{0\}-X\times\{\infty\})).
\end{align*}
Thus
\[
p_{1*}(W\cdot (X\times\{0\}-X\times\{\infty\}))= i_{E_0*}({\operatorname{div}} f_0)+i_{\hat{E}'*}({\operatorname{div}} f')-i_{E_\infty*}({\operatorname{div}} f_\infty)-i_{\hat{E}*}({\operatorname{div}} f),
\]
showing that $p_{1*}(|W|\cdot (X\times\{0\}-X\times\{\infty\}))$ is in $R^d(X, X^*)$, as desired.
<!-- end proof-10 -->
<!-- lemma-8: body_md -->
\label{lem:EtalePullback} Let $(X, X^*)$ and $(Y, Y^*)$ be admissible pairs with ${\operatorname{\rm dim}}_kX={\operatorname{\rm dim}}_kY=d$, and let $f:Y\to X$ be a morphism.  Suppose\\[5pt]
i.  $f^{-1}(X^*)\supset Y^*$ \\[2pt]
ii. $f$ is flat over $X\setminus X^*$\\[2pt]
iii. There is a closed subset $S\subset X^*\cap X(d)$ with ${\rm codim}_{X(d)}S\ge2$ and an open neighborhood $U$ of $f(Y^*)\cap X(d)^0\setminus S$ in $X(d)^0$  such that $f$ is flat over $U$.\\[5pt]
 Then
\begin{enumerate}
\item $f^{-1}(X\setminus X^*)\subset Y\setminus Y^*$.
\item For $z\in Z^d(X\setminus X^*)$, the pullback $f^*(z)$ is a well-defined 0-cycle on $Y$, supported in $Y\setminus Y^*$, giving the group homomorphism
\[
f^*:Z^d(X\setminus X^*)\to Z^d(Y\setminus Y^*)
\]
\item The homomorphism $f^*$ of (2) descends to a homomorphism
\[
f^*:{\operatorname{CH}}^d(X, X^*)\to {\operatorname{CH}}^d(Y, Y^*)
\]
\item Given a second admissible pair $(Z, Z^*)$, a morphism $g:Z\to Y$  and a closed subset $S'\subset Y(d)\cap Y^*$, satisfying (i)-(iii), there is a closed subset $S''$ of $X(d)\cap X^*$ such that  $fg:Z\to X$ and $S''$ satisfy (i)-(iii), hence $(fg)^*: {\operatorname{CH}}^d(X, X^*)\to {\operatorname{CH}}^d(Z, Z^*)$  is defined. Moreover,  we have
\[
(fg)^*=g^*f^*:{\operatorname{CH}}^d(X, X^*)\to {\operatorname{CH}}^d(Z, Z^*)
\]
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end lemma-8 -->
<!-- proof-11: body_md -->
(1) is our assumption (i) that $f^{-1}(X^*)\supset Y^*$. The assumption (ii) implies   (2) since we have a well-defined pullback map $f^*:Z^d(X\setminus X^*)\to Z^d(f^{-1}(X\setminus X^*))$, for the flat map $f:f^{-1}(X\setminus X^*)\to X\setminus X^*$, and we then apply (1), showing that $f^*(z)$ is supported in $Y\setminus Y^*$ if $z$ is in $Z^d(X\setminus X^*)$.

For (3), let  $T=X(d)\cap X(\le d-1)$. Then $T$ is a closed subset of $X^*\cap X(d)$, with ${\rm codim}_{X(d)}T\ge 2$;  note that $X(d)\setminus (S\cup T)=X(d)^0\setminus S$ is an open subset of $X(d)^0$; $f$ is flat over $U\setminus S$ by assumption.

By Lemma~\ref{lem:Mov1} we have
\[
R^d(X, X^*)=R^d(X, X^*)_{T\cup S},
\]
with $R^d(X, X^*)_{T\cup S}$ the subgroup of $Z^d(X\setminus X^*)$ generated by 0-cycles $i_{C*}({\operatorname{div}} h)$, where $i_C:C\to X$ is a Cartier curve on $X$ relative to $X^*$, $h\in {\mathcal O}_{C: C\cap X^*}^\times$, and $C$ is supported in $X(d)\setminus (S\cup T)=X(d)^0\setminus S$.
