\Pi_X:\amalg_{m,m'}{\operatorname{coeq}}_I(X,m)\times{\operatorname{coeq}}_I(X,m')\to{\operatorname{coeq}}_{II}(X)
\]
 denote the co-equalizer in ${\mathbf{Sets}}_*$ of the diagram \eqref{multline; coeqII}.  Recall the bijections $\Psi(X, m):{\operatorname{coeq}}_I(X, m)\xrightarrow{\sim} {\operatorname{\bf Vec}}_m(X)$, $m\ge0$, from Proposition~\ref{prop:VectmPresentation}. Then the diagram
\[
\xymatrix{
\amalg_{m,m'}{\operatorname{coeq}}_I(X,m)\times{\operatorname{coeq}}_I(X,m')\ar[r]^-{\Pi_X}\ar[d]^{\amalg_{m,m'}\Psi(X,m)\times\Psi(X,m')}&{\operatorname{coeq}}_{II}(X)\\
\amalg_{m,m'}{\operatorname{\bf Vec}}_m(X)\times{\operatorname{\bf Vec}}_{m'}(X)\ar[r]& K_0(X)
}
\]
induces a bijection of pointed sets ${\operatorname{coeq}}_{II}(X)\to K_0(X)$, natural in $X$.
<!-- end theorem-3 -->
<!-- proof-32: body_md -->
We need to see that the equivalence relation $\sim^*_{K_0}$ on $\amalg_{m,m'}{\operatorname{\bf Vec}}_m(X)\times{\operatorname{\bf Vec}}_{m'}(X)$ induced by   the relation
\begin{multline*}
(\Psi(X,m_1+m_t)\circ \oplus(s+q,1)_*(\psi, f_1),\Psi(X,m_2+m_t)\circ \oplus(t,2)_*(\psi, f_2))\\\sim^* (\Psi(X,m_1)\circ f_1, \Psi(X,m_2)\circ f_2)
\end{multline*}
for $\psi:X\to {\mathbb P}^N\times {{\mathcal F}{l}}(m_\bullet, M))$, $f_i:X\to {\mathbb P}^{N_i}\times{\operatorname{\rm Gr}}(m_i, M_i)$, agrees with the equivalence relation $\sim_{K_0}$. 

It follows from Lemma~\ref{lem:ExactSeqPresentation} that each short exact sequence 
\begin{equation}\label{eqn:TargetSeq}
0\to E_s\to E_t\to E_q\to 0
\end{equation}
of locally free coherent sheaves on $X$ arises (up to isomorphism) as $\psi^*(E_{m_\bullet, M}(-1))$ for a suitable $\psi:=(\iota, \phi)$, with $\iota:X\to {\mathbb P}^N$ corresponding to a choice of $N+1$ global generators for an invertible sheaf $L$,  $\phi:X\to {{\mathcal F}{l}}(m_\bullet, M)$ corresponding to the sequence of surjective maps ${\mathcal O}_X^M\to E_t\otimes L\to E_q\otimes L$ constructed from a choice of $M$ global generators for $E_t\otimes L$. Conversely, each $\psi:X\to {\mathbb P}^N\times {{\mathcal F}{l}}(m_\bullet, M)$ gives a corresponding exact sequence \eqref{eqn:TargetSeq} by taking $\psi^*(E_{m_\bullet, M}(-1))$, and these two operations are inverse to one another. 

Moreover,  given $\psi:X\to {\mathbb P}^N\times{{\mathcal F}{l}}(m_\bullet, M)$ as above,   locally free sheaves $E_i$ of ranks $m_i$, and globally generated invertible sheaves $L_i$ such that $E_i\otimes L_i$ is globally generated, $i=1,2$, we have the corresponding morphisms
\[
f_i:X\to {\mathbb P}^{N_i}\times{\operatorname{\rm Gr}}(m_i, M_i),\ i=1,2,
\]
by choosing a set of $M_i$ global generators for $E_i\otimes L_i$ and $N_i+1$ global generators for $L_i$. Applying Lemma~\ref{lem:ExactSeqPresentation} again, we  have
\[
\Psi(X, m_1+m_t)(\oplus(s+q,1)_*(\psi, f_1))=E_s\oplus E_q\oplus E_1,
\]
\[
\Psi(X, m_2+m_t)(\oplus(t,2)_*(\psi, f_2))= E_t\oplus E_2,
\]
and
\[
(\Psi(X,m_1)(f_1), \Psi(X, m_2)(f_2))= (E_1,E_2).
\]
Thus, the relation $\sim^*$ is given by
\[
(E_1, E_2)\sim^*(E_s\oplus E_q\oplus E_1, E_t\oplus E_2)
\]
for each $(E_1, E_2)\in {\operatorname{\bf Vec}}_{m_1}(X)\times{\operatorname{\bf Vec}}_{m_2}(X)$ and each short exact sequence $0\to E_s\to E_t\to E_q\to 0$ in ${\operatorname{\bf ses}}_m(X)$. It is then easy to see that  $\sim^*_{K_0}=\sim_{K_0}$.
<!-- end proof-32 -->
<!-- definition-15: body_md -->
Given morphisms $f_i:X\to {\mathbb P}^{N_i}\times{\operatorname{\rm Gr}}(m_i, M_i)$, $i=1,2$, we have the map to the product
\[
(f_1, f_2):X\to [{\mathbb P}^{N_1}\times{\operatorname{\rm Gr}}(m_1, M_1)]\times [{\mathbb P}^{N_2}\times{\operatorname{\rm Gr}}(m_2, M_2)].
\]
Let 
\[
p_1: [{\mathbb P}^{N_1}\times{\operatorname{\rm Gr}}(m_1, M_1)]\times [{\mathbb P}^{N_2}\times{\operatorname{\rm Gr}}(m_2, M_2)]\to
 {\mathbb P}^{N_1}\times{\operatorname{\rm Gr}}(m_1, M_1),
\] 
and
\[
p_2: [{\mathbb P}^{N_1}\times{\operatorname{\rm Gr}}(m_1, M_1)]\times [{\mathbb P}^{N_2}\times{\operatorname{\rm Gr}}(m_2, M_2)]\to
 {\mathbb P}^{N_2}\times{\operatorname{\rm Gr}}(m_2, M_2)
\] 
be the projections. 
 
 
We have the element 
\[
[p_1^*(E_{m_1, M_1}(-1))]-[p_2^*(E_{m_2, M_2}(-1))]\in K_0({\mathbb P}^{N_1}\times{\operatorname{\rm Gr}}(m_1, M_1)\times {\mathbb P}^{N_2}\times{\operatorname{\rm Gr}}(m_2, M_2))
\]
and its Chern class
\[
c_d([p_1^*(E_{m_1, M_1}(-1))]-[p_2^*(E_{m_2, M_2}(-1))])\in {\operatorname{CH}}^d({\mathbb P}^{N_1}\times{\operatorname{\rm Gr}}(m_1, M_1)\times {\mathbb P}^{N_2}\times{\operatorname{\rm Gr}}(m_2, M_2)).
\]
Define $c_d(f_1-f_2)\in {\operatorname{CH}}^d(X, X^*)$  by
\[
c_d(f_1-f_2):=(f_1, f_2)^*(c_d([p_1^*(E_{m_1, M_1}(-1))]-[p_2^*(E_{m_2, M_2}(-1))])).
\]
<!-- end definition-15 -->
<!-- lemma-22: body_md -->
\label{lem:Compatibility} Let  $f_i:X\to {\mathbb P}^{N_i}\times{\operatorname{\rm Gr}}(m_i, M_i)$ be morphisms, $i=1,2$.\\[5pt]
1. Given  elements $g_i\in \operatorname{GL}_{N_i+1}(k)\times\operatorname{GL}_{M_i}(k)$, $i=1,2$, we have
\[
c_d(f_1-f_2)=c_d(g_1\cdot f_1-g_2\cdot f_2)\text{ in }{\operatorname{CH}}^d(X, X^*).
\]
2. Given $M_i'\ge M_i$, $N_i'\ge N_i$, $i=1,2$, we have the closed immersions $i_{m_i, M_i', M_i}:{\operatorname{\rm Gr}}(m_i, M_i)\to {\operatorname{\rm Gr}}(m_i, M_i')$, $i_{N_i', N_i}:{\mathbb P}^{N_i}\to {\mathbb P}^{N_i'}$, giving the morphisms
\[
f_i':X\to {\mathbb P}^{N_i'}\times {\operatorname{\rm Gr}}(m_i, M_i'),\ f_i':=(i_{N_i', N_i}\times i_{m, M_i', M_i})\circ f_i,\ i=1,2.
\]
Then
\[
c_d(f_1'-f_2')=c_d(f_1-f_2)\text{ in }{\operatorname{CH}}^d(X, X^*).
\]
3. For $i=1,2$, let $E_i$ be a locally free sheaf on $X$ of rank $m_i$, let $L_i$ be an invertible sheaf on $X$ and let $\varpi_i:{\mathcal O}_X^{N_i+1}\to L_i$, $\pi_i:{\mathcal O}_X^{M_i}\to E_i\otimes L_i$,  be surjections, such that $p_1\circ f_i$ classifies $\varpi_i$ and $p_2\circ f_i$ classifies $\pi_i$. Suppose we have another pair of surjections $\varpi_i':{\mathcal O}_X^{N_i'+1}\to L_i$, $\pi_i':{\mathcal O}_X^{M_i'}\to E_i\otimes L_i$, giving a second pair of maps
\[
f_i':X\to {\mathbb P}^{N_i'}\times{\operatorname{\rm Gr}}(m_i, M_i'),\ i=1,2.
\]
Then
\[
c_d(f_1'-f_2')=c_d(f_1-f_2)\text{ in }{\operatorname{CH}}^d(X, X^*).
\]
4. Take integers $N_i, N_i', M_i>0$, $i=1, 2$ and an integer $m>0$. Consider the maps
\eqref{Veronese2}
\[
\lambda_i:=\lambda_{N_i, N_i', m,M_i}:{\mathbb P}^{N_i}\times{\mathbb P}^{N_i'}\times{\operatorname{\rm Gr}}(m, M_i)\to {\mathbb P}^{N_i''}\times {\operatorname{\rm Gr}}(m, M_i''),
\]
with $M_i''=(N_i'+1)\cdot M_i$, $N_i''=(N_i+1)\cdot(N_i'+1)-1$, $i=1,2$. We also have the projections
\[
p_{13,i}:{\mathbb P}^{N_i}\times{\mathbb P}^{N_i'}\times{\operatorname{\rm Gr}}(m, M_i)\to {\mathbb P}^{N_i}\times{\operatorname{\rm Gr}}(m, M_i),\ i=1,2.
\]
Let $g_i:X\to {\mathbb P}^{N_i}\times{\mathbb P}^{N_i'}\times{\operatorname{\rm Gr}}(m, M_i)$ be morphisms, $i=1,2$, and let
\[
f_i=p_{13,i}\circ g_i:X\to  {\mathbb P}^{N_i}\times{\operatorname{\rm Gr}}(m, M_i),\ f_i'=\lambda_i\circ g_i:X\to {\mathbb P}^{N_i''}\times {\operatorname{\rm Gr}}(m, M_i''),\ i=1,2.
\]
Then
\[
c_d(f_1-f_2)=c_d(f_1'-f_2')\text{ in }{\operatorname{CH}}^d(X, X^*).
\]
5. Take non-negative integers $N, N_1, N_2$, $m_\bullet:=(m_t,m_q)$, $M$, $m_1$, $M_1$, $m_2$, $M_2$, with $m_t\ge m_q$, and choose an integer $r\gg0$ satisfying \eqref{eqn:TwistConditions} for $(m_\bullet, M)$.    Let $N(m_\bullet, M,r)=(N(m_t, M,r)+1)(N(m_q, M,r)+1)-1$. Recall from \eqref{eqn:ChosenSurjections} the integer $M_t$, and from Definition~\ref{def:TotalAndSum} the integers $M_t^*:=M_t\cdot(N(m_\bullet, M,r)+1)$,  $N^*_i=(N(m_\bullet, M,r)+1)(N_i+1)-1$,  $M_i^*:=M_i\cdot (N_i+1)$, $i=1,2$, and the morphisms
\[
\oplus(s+q,1):{\mathbb P}^N\times {{\mathcal F}{l}}(m_\bullet, M)\times{\mathbb P}^{N_1}\times{\operatorname{\rm Gr}}(m_1, M_1) \to {\mathbb P}^{N^*_1}\times{\operatorname{\rm Gr}}(m_t+m_1, M_t^*+M_1^*)
\]
and
\[
\oplus(t,2):{\mathbb P}^N\times {{\mathcal F}{l}}(m_\bullet, M)\times{\mathbb P}^{N_2}\times{\operatorname{\rm Gr}}(m_2, M_2) \to {\mathbb P}^{N^*_2}\times{\operatorname{\rm Gr}}(m_t+m_2, M_t^*+M_2^*).
\]
Take morphisms
\[
f_i:X\to {\mathbb P}^{N_i}\times{\operatorname{\rm Gr}}(m_i, M_i), i=1,2,
\]
and
\[
\psi:X\to {\mathbb P}^N\times {{\mathcal F}{l}}(m_\bullet, M),
\]
and let
\[
f_1':=\oplus(s+q,1)\circ (\psi, f_1):X\to {\mathbb P}^{N^*_1}\times{\operatorname{\rm Gr}}(m_t+m_1, M_t^*+M_1^*),
\]
\[
 f_2'=\oplus(t,2)\circ (\psi, f_2):X\to {\mathbb P}^{N^*_2}\times{\operatorname{\rm Gr}}(m_t+m_2, M_t^*+M_2^*).
\]
Then 
\[
c_d(f_1-f_2)=c_d(f_1'-f_2')\text{ in }{\operatorname{CH}}^d(X, X^*).
\]
<!-- end lemma-22 -->
<!-- proof-33: body_md -->
The fact that $\operatorname{GL}_{N_1+1}(k)\times\operatorname{GL}_{M_1}(k)\times \operatorname{GL}_{N_2+1}(k)\times\operatorname{GL}_{M_2}(k)$ acts trivially on ${\operatorname{CH}}^*({\mathbb P}^{N_1}\times{\operatorname{\rm Gr}}(m_1, M_1)\times {\mathbb P}^{N_2}\times{\operatorname{\rm Gr}}(m_2, M_2))$ yields  (1). 

For (2), the closed immersions $i_{m_i, M_i', M_i}$, $i_{N_i', N_i}$ are equivariant with respect to the evident homomorphisms of general linear groups, so (2) follows from Proposition~\ref{prop:HomogFunctoriality}, and the fact that for 
\[
\iota:= i_{N_1',N_1}\times i_{m_1, M_1', M_1}\times  i_{N_2',N_2}\times i_{m_2, M_2', M_2}
\]
we have
\begin{multline*}
\iota^*(c_d([p_1^*(E_{m_1, M_1'}(-1))]-[p_2^*(E_{m_2, M_2'}(-1))]))\\=
c_d([p_1^*(E_{m_1, M_1}(-1))]-[p_2^*(E_{m_2, M_2}(-1))])
\end{multline*}

For (3), suppose $\pi_i$ is given by the global sections $h_{i,1},\ldots, h_{i, M_i}$ of $E_i\otimes L_i$ and $\pi_i'$ is given by the global sections $h_{i,1}',\ldots, h_{i, M_i'}'$ of $E_i\otimes L_i$, $i=1,2$.  Let $\pi_i''$ be given by the global sections $h_{i,1},\ldots, h_{i, M_i}, h_{i,1}',\ldots, h_{i, M_i'}'$.
Similarly, if $\varpi_i$ is given by global sections $s_{i,0},\ldots, s_{i, N_i}$ of $L_i$ and $\varpi_i'$ is given by the global sections $s_{i,0}',\ldots, s_{i, N_i'}'$ of $L_i$, $i=1,2$, let $\varpi_i''$ be given by global sections $s_{i,0},\ldots, s_{i, N_i}, s_{i,0}',\ldots, s_{i, N_i'}'$. Let $M_i''=M_i+M_i'$, $N_i''=N_i+N_i'+1$, and let
\[
f_i'':X\to {\mathbb P}^{N_i''}\times {\operatorname{\rm Gr}}(m, M_i'')
\]
be the map given by the surjections $\varpi_i''$ and $\pi_i''$. Clearly, it suffices to compare $c_d(f_1-f_2)$ and $c_d(f_1''-f_2'')$. 

We have the inclusions $i_{m, M_i'', M_i}:{\operatorname{\rm Gr}}(m, M_i)\to {\operatorname{\rm Gr}}(m, M_i'')$ and $i_{N_i'', N_i}:{\mathbb P}^{N_i}\to {\mathbb P}^{N_i''}$. Let $\iota_i=i_{N_i'', N_i}\times i_{m, M_i'', M_i}$. 
Using (2), it suffices to show 
\[
c_d(\iota_1\circ f_1-\iota_2\circ f_2)=c_d(f_1''-f_2'')
\]
For this, let $t_0, t_1$ be standard homogeneous coordinates on ${\mathbb P}^1$, with $0=[1:0]$ and $\infty=[0:1]$. We have the locally free sheaves $E_i(1)$ on $X\times{\mathbb P}^1$, with generating global sections
\[
(t_0+t_1)h_{i,1},\ldots, (t_0+t_1)h_{i, M_i}, t_1h_{i,1}',\ldots, t_1h_{i, M_i'}'
\]
for $E_i(1)\otimes L_i$ and similarly, we have the invertible sheaves $L_i(1)$ on $X\times{\mathbb P}^1$ with
generating global sections
\[
(t_0+t_1)s_{i,0},\ldots, (t_0+t_1)s_{i, N_i}, t_1s_{i,0}',\ldots, t_1s_{i, N_i'}'
\]
 Letting 
\[
F_i:X\times{\mathbb P}^1\to {\mathbb P}^{N_i}\times{\operatorname{\rm Gr}}(m, M_i'')
\]
be the corresponding morphism, we have 
\[
F_i|_{X\times\{0\}}=\iota_i\circ f_i, \ F_i|_{X\times\{\infty\}}=f_i'',\ i=1,2,
\]
after choosing trivializations of ${\mathcal O}_{{\mathbb P}^1}(1)$ at $0$ and $\infty$. By Proposition~\ref{prop:RatEquivPullback}, we have
\[
c_d(F_1|_{X\times\{0\}}-F_2|_{X\times\{0\}})=c_d(F_1|_{X\times\{\infty\}}-F_2|_{X\times\{\infty\}}),
\]
proving (3).

To prove (4), Lemma~\ref{lem:TensorIdentity} gives us the isomorphism of locally free sheaves on 
${\mathbb P}^{N_i}\times{\mathbb P}^{N_i'}\times{\operatorname{\rm Gr}}(m, M_i)$,
\[
p_{13,i}^*(E_{m, M_i}(-1))\cong \lambda_i^*(E_{m, M_i''}(-1)),\ i=1,2,
\]
so
\[
c_d([p_{13,1}^*(E_{m, M_1}(-1))]-[p_{13,2}^*(E_{m, M_2}(-1))])=
c_d([\lambda_1^*(E_{m, M_1''}(-1))]-[\lambda_2^*(E_{m, M_2''}(-1))])
\]
in ${\operatorname{CH}}^d({\mathbb P}^{N_i}\times{\mathbb P}^{N_i'}\times{\operatorname{\rm Gr}}(m, M_i))$. On the other hand, the morphism $p_{13,i}$ is equivariant with respect to the projection
\[
p_{13}: \operatorname{GL}_{N_i+1}\times \operatorname{GL}_{N_i'+1}\times \operatorname{GL}_{M_i}\to \operatorname{GL}_{N_i+1}\times \operatorname{GL}_{M_i}
\]
and $\lambda_i$ is equivariant with respect to 
\[
\rho_i=(\rho_{\otimes,N_i+1, N_i'+1}\circ p_{12},  \rho_{\otimes,N'_i+1, M_i}\circ p_{23}:\operatorname{GL}_{N_i+1}\times \operatorname{GL}_{N_i'+1}\times \operatorname{GL}_{M_i}\to \operatorname{GL}_{N_i''}\times \operatorname{GL}_{M_i''}
\]
where $\rho_{\otimes, N, M}:\operatorname{GL}_N\times \operatorname{GL}_M\to \operatorname{GL}_{NM}$ is the tensor product representation (in suitable coordinates). Thus, by Proposition~\ref{prop:HomogFunctoriality}, we have
\begin{align*}
c_d(f_1'-f_2')&=(f_1', f_2')^*(c_d([p_1^*(E_{m_1, M''_1}(-1))]-[p_2^*(E_{m_2, M''_2}(-1))]))\\
&=(g_1, g_2)^*(c_d([\lambda_1^*(E_{m, M_1''}(-1))]-[\lambda_2^*(E_{m, M_1''}(-1))]))\\
&=(g_1, g_2)^*(c_d([p_{13,1}^*(E_{m, M_1}(-1))]-[p_{13,2}^*(E_{m, M_2}(-1))]))\\
&=(f_1, f_2)^*(c_d([E_{m, M_1}(-1)]-[E_{m, M_2}(-1)]))\\
&=c_d(f_1-f_2),
\end{align*}
proving (4).

For (5), we have the universal exact sequence
\begin{equation}\label{eqn:UnivExactSeq}
0\to E_{m_\bullet, M}^s\to E_{m_\bullet, M}^t\to E_{m_\bullet, M}^q\to0
\end{equation}
on ${{\mathcal F}{l}}(m_\bullet, M)$. It follows from Lemma~\ref{lem:TwistedDirectSum} and the definition of the maps $\oplus(s+q,1)$ and $\oplus(t,2)$ (Definition~\ref{def:TotalAndSum}) that
\begin{multline*}
\oplus(s+q,1)^*(E_{m_t+m_1, M_t^*+M_1^*}(-1))\\\cong p_{12}^*(E_{m_\bullet, M}^s(-1,0)\oplus E_{m_\bullet, M}^q(-1,0))\oplus p_{34}^*(E_{m_1, M_1}(-1))
\end{multline*}
and
\[
\oplus(t,2)^*(E_{m_t+m_2, M_t^*+M_2^*}(-1))\cong p_{12}^*(E_{m_\bullet, M}^t(-1,0))\oplus p_{34}^*(E_{m_2, M_2}(-1))
\]
Let
\[
Y=[{\mathbb P}^N\times {{\mathcal F}{l}}(m_\bullet, M)]\times[{\mathbb P}^{N_1}\times{\operatorname{\rm Gr}}(m_1, M_1)] \times[{\mathbb P}^{N_2}\times{\operatorname{\rm Gr}}(m_2, M_2)], 
\]
with projections
\[
p_0:Y\to {\mathbb P}^N\times {{\mathcal F}{l}}(m_\bullet, M),\ p_1:Y\to {\mathbb P}^{N_1}\times{\operatorname{\rm Gr}}(m_1, M_1),\ p_2:Y\to 
{\mathbb P}^{N_2}\times{\operatorname{\rm Gr}}(m_2, M_2),
\]
and corresponding projections $p_{ij}$, $0\le i<j\le 2$.
Using the exact sequence \eqref{eqn:UnivExactSeq}, we have the relation in $K_0(Y)$
\begin{multline*}
[p_{01}^*(\oplus(s+q,1)^*(E_{m_t+m_1, M_t^*+M_1^*}(-1)))]-
[p_{02}^*(\oplus(t,2)^*(E_{m_t+m_2, M_t^*+M_2^*}(-1)))]\\=
[p_{1}^*(E_{m_1, M_1}(-1))]-[p_{2}^*(E_{m_1, M_1}(-1))], 
\end{multline*}
giving the relation in ${\operatorname{CH}}^d(Y)$
\begin{multline*}
c_d([p_{01}^*(\oplus(s+q,1)^*(E_{m_t+m_1, M_t^*+M_1^*}(-1)))]-
[p_{02}^*(\oplus(t,2)^*(E_{m_t+m_2, M_t^*+M_2^*}(-1)))])\\=
c_d([p_{1}^*(E_{m_1, M_1}(-1))]-[p_{2}^*(E_{m_2, M_2}(-1))])
\end{multline*}

We   have the map $(\psi, f_1, f_2):X\to Y$ with
\[
\oplus(s+q,1)\circ p_{01}\circ (\psi, f_1, f_2)=f_1',\ \oplus(t,2)\circ p_{02}\circ (\psi, f_1, f_2)=f_2',
\]
and
\[
p_{1}\circ (\psi, f_1, f_2)=f_1, \ p_{2}\circ (\psi,f_1,f_2)=f_2.
\]
Applying the functoriality statement of  Proposition~\ref{prop:HomogFunctoriality}  gives
\begin{align*}
c_d(f_1-f_2)&= (\psi, f_1, f_2)^*(c_d([p_{1}^*(E_{m_1, M_1}(-1))]-[p_{2}^*(E_{m_2, M_2}(-1))])\\
&=(\psi, f_1, f_2)^*c_d\Big([p_{01}^*(\oplus(s+q,1)^*(E_{m_t+m_1, M_t^*+M_1^*}(-1)))]\\&\hskip 100pt-
[p_{02}^*(\oplus(t,2)^*(E_{m_t+m_2, M_t^*+M_2^*}(-1)))]\Big)\\
&=c_d(f_1'-f_2')
\end{align*}
<!-- end proof-33 -->
<!-- theorem-4: body_md -->
\label{thm:TopChernClass} Let $k$ be  infinite field, let $(X, X^*)$ be an admissible pair over $k$, and let $d={\operatorname{\rm dim}}_kX$.  Then there is a map of pointed sets
\[
c_d:K_0(X)\to {\operatorname{CH}}^d(X, X^*),
\]
uniquely determined by the identity
\begin{equation}\label{eqn:CharId}
c_d([f_1^*(E_{m_1, M_1}(-1))]-[f_2^*(E_{m_2, M_2}(-1))])=c_d(f_1-f_2)
\end{equation}
for morphisms $f_i:X\to {\mathbb P}^{N_i}\times{\operatorname{\rm Gr}}(m_i, M_i)$, $i=1,2$.
<!-- end theorem-4 -->
<!-- proof-34: body_md -->
Breaking up $X$ into its connected components and discarding those of dimension $<d$, we may assume that $X$ is connected. We have the map of sets
\begin{multline*}
\amalg_{N_1, m_1, M_1, N_2, m_2, M_2}{\rm Hom}(X,{\mathbb P}^{N_1}\times{\operatorname{\rm Gr}}(m_1, M_1))\times {\rm Hom}(X,{\mathbb P}^{N_2}\times{\operatorname{\rm Gr}}(m_2, M_2))\\
\xrightarrow{c_d^{(0)}}{\operatorname{CH}}^d(X, X^*)
\end{multline*}
sending $(f_1, f_2)$ to $(f_1, f_2)^*(c_d([p_{12}^*(E_{m_1, M_1}(-1))]-[p_{34}^*(E_{m_2, M_2}(-1))]))$.
\\[5pt]
 {\bf Step 1} The map $c_d^{(0)}$
descends to a well-defined map of sets
\begin{multline*}
\amalg_{N_1, m_1, M_1, N_2, m_2, M_2}\underline{{\rm Hom}}(X,{\mathbb P}^{N_1}\times{\operatorname{\rm Gr}}(m_1, M_1))\times \underline{\rm Hom}(X,{\mathbb P}^{N_2}\times{\operatorname{\rm Gr}}(m_2, M_2))\\
\xrightarrow{c_d^{(1)}} {\operatorname{CH}}^d(X, X^*)
\end{multline*}
This follows from Lemma~\ref{lem:Compatibility}(1)-(3).\\[5pt]
{\bf Step 2} The map $c_d^{(1)}$ descends to a map of pointed sets
\[
c_d^{(2)}:\amalg_{m_1, m_2}{\operatorname{\bf Vec}}_{m_1}(X)\times{\operatorname{\bf Vec}}_{m_2}(X)\to {\operatorname{CH}}^d(X, X^*)
\]
via the surjection of Proposition~\ref{prop:VectmPresentation}, where  $*={\operatorname{\bf Vec}}_{0}(X)\times{\operatorname{\bf Vec}}_{0}(X)$ is the base-point on the source, and $0$ is the base-point on the target.  This follows from 
Proposition~\ref{prop:VectmPresentation} and Lemma~\ref{lem:Compatibility}(4).\\[5pt]
{\bf Step 3} The map $c_d^{(2)}$ descends to a well-defined map of pointed sets
\[
c_d:K_0(X)\to {\operatorname{CH}}^d(X, X^*)
\]
via the surjection of Theorem~\ref{thm:K0Presentation}. This follows from Theorem~\ref{thm:K0Presentation} and Lemma~\ref{lem:Compatibility}(5).

The fact that $c_d$  satisfies the identity \eqref{eqn:CharId} follows from the definition of $c_d^{(0)}$. The identity \eqref{eqn:CharId} determines $c_d$ uniquely since $K_0(X)$ is generated by formal differences of classes $[E_1]-[E_2]$, for $E_1, E_2$ locally free coherent sheaves, and for each $E_1, E_2$, there are morphisms $f_i:X\to {\mathbb P}^{N_i}\times {\operatorname{\rm Gr}}(m_i, M_i)$, $i=1,2$ with $E_i\cong f_i^*(E_{m_i, M_i}(-1))$, $i=1,2$.
<!-- end proof-34 -->
<!-- remark-17: body_md -->
\label{rem:ChernClassRegular} Let $Y\in{\operatorname{\mathbf{Sch}}}^{\operatorname{\text{\rm qp}}}_k$ be a regular scheme, $n>0$ an integer. We have the Chern class map $c_n:K_0(Y)\to {\operatorname{CH}}^n(Y)$ defined using  Fulton's Chern class operators $c_n^F(-)\cap -$  \cite[\S 3.2, Example 3.2.7]{Fulton}, 
\[
c_n(x):=c_n^F(x)\cap [Y], 
\]
where $[Y]\in {\operatorname{CH}}_*(Y)$ is the fundamental class. In case $Y$ is smooth over $k$, this is the same as the usual Chern class map defined by Grothendieck;  see Remark~\ref{rem:FultonChernClass} for further details.
<!-- end remark-17 -->
<!-- proposition-10: body_md -->
\label{prop:ChernClassFunct} Let $(X, X^*)$ be an admissible pair over an infinite field $k$, and let $d={\operatorname{\rm dim}}_kX$.\\[5pt]
1. Let $(Y, Y^*)$ be a second admissible pair with ${\operatorname{\rm dim}}_kY=d$ and let $f:Y\to X$ be a morphism.  Suppose that the conditions (i)-(iii) of Lemma~\ref{lem:EtalePullback} are satisfied, giving the pullback map $f^*:{\operatorname{CH}}^d(X, X^*)\to {\operatorname{CH}}^d(Y, Y^*)$. Then the diagram
\[
\xymatrix{
K_0(X)\ar[r]^-{f^*}\ar[d]^{c_d}&K_0(Y)\ar[d]^{c_d}\\
{\operatorname{CH}}^d(X,X^*)\ar[r]^-{f^*}&{\operatorname{CH}}^d(Y, Y^*)
}
\]
commutes.\\[5pt]
2. Let $f:Y\to X$ be a morphism, where  $Y\in{\operatorname{\mathbf{Sch}}}_k^{\operatorname{\text{\rm qp}}}$ is regular and of pure dimension $d$ over $k$. We have the Chern class map $c_d:K_0(Y)\to {\operatorname{CH}}^d(Y)$ of Remark~\ref{rem:ChernClassRegular}.
Suppose that $f$ is flat over $X\setminus X^*$, giving the pullback map $f^*:{\operatorname{CH}}^d(X,X^*)\to {\operatorname{CH}}^d(Y)$, following Remark~\ref{rem:OpenIm}(2).   Then the diagram
\[
\xymatrix{
K_0(X)\ar[r]^-{f^*}\ar[d]^{c_d}&K_0(Y)\ar[d]^{c_d}\\
{\operatorname{CH}}^d(X,X^*)\ar[r]^-{f^*}&{\operatorname{CH}}^d(Y)
}
\]
commutes.  
\\[5pt]
3. Let $k\hookrightarrow F$ be an extension of fields. Suppose that the base-extension $X_F$ is reduced and $X_F\setminus (X^*)_F$ is regular, giving the pullback map (Lemma~\ref{lem:base-change})
\[
p_X^*:{\operatorname{CH}}^d(X, X^*)\to {\operatorname{CH}}^d(X_F, X_F^*).
\]
Then the diagram 
\[
\xymatrix{
K_0(X)\ar[r]^-{p_X^*}\ar[d]^{c_d}&K_0(X_F)\ar[d]^{c_d}\\
{\operatorname{CH}}^d(X,X^*)\ar[r]^-{p_X^*}&{\operatorname{CH}}^d(X_F, X_F^*)
}
\]
commutes.
<!-- end proposition-10 -->
<!-- proof-35: body_md -->
For (1),  we reduce to showing that, given morphisms $f_i:X\to {\mathbb P}^{N_i}\times{\operatorname{\rm Gr}}(m_i, M_i)$, $i=1,2$, we have
\[
f^*(c_d(f_1-f_2))=c_d((f_1f)-(f_2f)).
\]
We have
\begin{align*}
f^*(c_d(f_1-f_2))&=f^*(f_1, f_2)^*c_d([p_{1}^*E_{m_1, M_1}(-1)]- [p_{2}^*E_{m_2, M_2}(-1)])\\
&=(f_1f, f_2f)^*c_d([p_{1}^*E_{m_1, M_1}(-1)]- [p_{2}^*E_{m_2, M_2}(-1)])\\
&=c_d((f_1f)-(f_2f)),
\end{align*}
where we use Proposition~\ref{prop:PullbackFunct3} for the second identity.  

For (2), we claim that $c_d:K_0(Y)\to {\operatorname{CH}}^d(Y)$, defined using Fulton's Chern class operators,  agrees with the Chern class map defined via Theorem~\ref{thm:TopChernClass} for the admissible pair $(Y,\0)$. Accepting the claim, (2) is a special case of (1),  using Remark~\ref{rem:OpenIm} to note that the pullback map $f^*:{\operatorname{CH}}^d(X, X^*)\to {\operatorname{CH}}^d(Y)$ is defined as a special case of the pullback map constructed in Lemma~\ref{lem:EtalePullback}, with $Y^*=\0$. 


To prove the claim, we need only check that for $(f_1, f_2):Y\to {\mathbb P}^{N_1}\times{\operatorname{\rm Gr}}(m_1,M_1)\times {\mathbb P}^{N_2}\times{\operatorname{\rm Gr}}(m_2,M_2)=:H$ a morphism, that 
\begin{multline*}
c_d^F((f_1, f_2)^*([p_1^*(E_{m_1, M_1}(-1))]-[p_2^*(E_{m_2, M_2}(-1)]))\cap [Y]\\=
(f_1, f_2)^*(c_d([p_1^*(E_{m_1, M_1}(-1))]-[p_2^*(E_{m_2, M_2}(-1))])).
\end{multline*}
This is \eqref{eqn:BivChernClass} with $\alpha=[H]$, together with \eqref{eqn:ChernClassLciPullback}.

The proof of (3) is similar to the proof of (1). Given morphisms $f_i:X\to {\mathbb P}^{N_i}_k\times{\operatorname{\rm Gr}}_k(m_i, M_i)$, $i=1,2$, we have the induced morphisms $f_{iF}:X_F\to {\mathbb P}_F^{N_i}\times{\operatorname{\rm Gr}}_F(m_i, M_i)$, $i=1,2$. If we have an algebraic cycle 
\[
Z\in {\operatorname{CH}}^d({\mathbb P}^{N_1}_k\times{\operatorname{\rm Gr}}_k(m_1, M_1)\times {\mathbb P}^{N_2}_k\times{\operatorname{\rm Gr}}_k(m_2, M_2))
\]
representing $c_d([p_{1}^*E_{m_1, M_1}(-1)]- [p_{2}^*E_{m_2, M_2}(-1)]))$, then the base-change 
\[
Z_F\in 
{\operatorname{CH}}^d({\mathbb P}^{N_1}_F\times{\operatorname{\rm Gr}}_F(m_1, M_1)\times {\mathbb P}^{N_2}_F\times{\operatorname{\rm Gr}}_F(m_2, M_2)
\]
represents $c_d([p_{1}^*E^F_{m_1, M_1}(-1)]- [p_{2}^*E^F_{m_2, M_2}(-1)]))$, where $E^F_{m_1, M_1}$, $E^F_{m_2, M_2}$ are the respective base-changes of $E^F_{m_1, M_1}$, $E^F_{m_2, M_2}$. If  the pullback $(f_1, f_2)^*(Z)$ is well-defined, so that $c_d(f_1-f_2)$ is represented by  $(f_{1}, f_{2})^*(Z)$, then the pull-back $(f_{1F}, f_{2F})^*(Z_F)$ is also well-defined, and  $c_d(f_{1F}-f_{2F})$ is therefore represented by $(f_{1F}, f_{2F})^*(Z_F)$. Since
$(f_{1F}, f_{2F})^*(Z_F)=p_X^*(f_1, f_2)^*(Z)$ as cycles, we thus have
\[
c_d(f_{1F}-f_{2F})=p_X^*(c_d(f_1-f_2))\in {\operatorname{CH}}^*(X_F, X_F^*),
\]
which suffices to prove (3).
<!-- end proof-35 -->
<!-- proposition-11: body_md -->
\label{prop:CycleClass} Let $(X, X^*)$ be an admissible pair and let $d={\operatorname{\rm dim}}_kX$. 
Then the group homomorphism
\[
{\rm cl}^d:Z^d(X\setminus X^*)\to K_0(X)
\]
sending a closed point $x\in X\setminus X^*$ to the $K_0$-class of the residue field $k(x)$, viewed as a coherent ${\mathcal O}_X$-module of finite homological dimension, descends to a well-defined group homomorphism
\[
{\rm cl}^d:{\operatorname{CH}}^d(X, X^*)\to K_0(X)
\]
with image $F^dK_0(X)$.
<!-- end proposition-11 -->
<!-- proof-36: body_md -->
Take $Y\subset X$ with $X\setminus Y$ regular. It is shown in \cite[Proposition 2.1]{LW} that the map $Z_0(X\setminus Y)\to K_0(X)$ sending $x$ to the $K_0$-class of the residue field $k(x)$ descends to a well-defined homomorphism ${\rm cl}_0:{\operatorname{CH}}_0(X,Y)\to K_0(X)$.  There is a tacit assumption that $X\setminus Y$ is dense in $X$, but this is not needed for the proof, so is also applicable to ${\operatorname{CH}}^d(X, X^*)$, via Proposition~\ref{prop:Comparison}(2).

It remains to show that ${\rm cl}^d$ has image $F^dK_0(X)$. For this,  it is clear that ${\rm cl}^d({\operatorname{CH}}^d(X, X^*))$ is the subgroup of $K_0(X)$ generated by classes $[k(x)]$ for $x$ a closed point in $X\setminus X^*$, which is $F^dK_0(X)$ in case $X^*=X_{\rm sing}\cup X(\le d-1)$. However, by Lemma~\ref{lem:CHSurj}, the map
\[
{\operatorname{CH}}^d(X, X^*)\to {\operatorname{CH}}^d(X, X_{\rm sing}\cup X(\le d-1))
\]
induced by the inclusion $X_{\rm sing}\cup X(\le d-1))\subset X^*$ is surjective. Since  the diagram
\[
\xymatrix{
{\operatorname{CH}}^d(X, X^*)\ar[r]\ar[dr]_{{\rm cl}^d}& {\operatorname{CH}}^d(X, X_{\rm sing}\cup X(\le d-1))\ar[d]^{{\rm cl}^d}\\
&K_0(X)
}
\]
commutes, we have ${\rm cl}^d({\operatorname{CH}}^d(X, X^*))=F^dK_0(X)$.
<!-- end proof-36 -->
<!-- theorem-5: body_md -->
\label{thm:RR} Let $k$ be an infinite field and let $(X, X^*)$ be an admissible pair over $k$.  Then 
\begin{enumerate}
\item The restriction of $c_d$ to $F^dK_0(X)$ is a homomorphism of abelian groups
\[
c_d:F^dK_0(X)\to {\operatorname{CH}}^d(X, X^*).
\]
\item We have
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(a)] $c_d\circ {\rm cl}^d=(-1)^{d-1}(d-1)!\cdot{\operatorname{\rm Id}}_{{\operatorname{CH}}^d(X, X^*)}$,
\item[(b)] ${\rm cl}^d\circ c_d=(-1)^{d-1}(d-1)!\cdot{\operatorname{\rm Id}}_{F^dK_0(X)}$.
\end{enumerate}
\end{enumerate}
In particular, the homomorphisms ${\rm cl}^d:{\operatorname{CH}}^d(X, X^*)\to F^dK_0(X)$ and $c_d:F^dK_0(X)\to {\operatorname{CH}}^d(X, X^*)$ both have kernels that are killed by $(d-1)!$.
<!-- end theorem-5 -->
<!-- proof-37: body_md -->
Note first that (1) is a consequence of (2a). Indeed, by Proposition~\ref{prop:CycleClass}, the map
\[
{\rm cl}^d:{\operatorname{CH}}^d(X, X^*)\to F^dK_0(X)
\]
is a surjective group homomorphism, and if we know that 
\[
c_d\circ {\rm cl}^d=(-1)^{d-1}(d-1)!\cdot{\operatorname{\rm Id}}_{{\operatorname{CH}}^d(X, X^*)}, 
\]
it follows that $c_d\circ {\rm cl}^d$ is a group homomorphism, which implies that $c_d$ is itself also a group homomorphism.

Similarly, the identity (2a) implies the identity (2b) by   applying composition $-\circ {\rm cl}^d$ with the surjective homomorphism ${\rm cl}^d$. 


It thus remains to prove (2a).

Let  $j:X\to \bar{X}$ be a projective closure of $X$ and let $\bar{X}^*\supset \bar{X}_{\rm sing}\cup \bar{X}(d-1)$ be a closed subset with ${\operatorname{\rm dim}}_k\bar{X}^*<d$ and with $j^{-1}(\bar{X}^*)=X^*$; since the closure of a reduced scheme is reduced, $\bar{X}(d)^0$ is reduced. Then $(\bar{X}, \bar{X}^*)$ is an admissible pair with $j(X\setminus X^*)\subset \bar{X}\setminus \bar{X}^*$. We have a well-defined pushforward map
\[
j_*:Z^d(X\setminus X^*)\to Z^d(\bar{X}\setminus \bar{X}^*),
\]
even though $j$ is not proper, and we have $j^*:K_0(\bar{X})\to K_0(X)$, with
\[
j^*({\rm cl}^d(j_*(z)))={\rm cl}^d(z)\in K_0(X)
\]
for $z\in Z^d(X\setminus X^*)$. We also have the pullback map $j^*:{\operatorname{CH}}^d(\bar{X}, \bar{X}^*)\to {\operatorname{CH}}^d(X, X^*)$ by Remark~\ref{rem:OpenIm}, with  $j^*[j_*(z)]=[z]$. We can apply Proposition~\ref{prop:ChernClassFunct}(1),  which gives the identity 
\[
j^*(c_d([j_*(z)]))=c_d(j^*[j_*(z)])=c_d([z]).
\]
Thus,  we may assume from the start that $X$ is projective. 

Suppose we have $z=\sum_{i=1}^s r_ix_i\in Z_0(X\setminus X^*)$ with the $x_i$ distinct and each $r_i\neq0$. We proceed by induction on $s$, the case $s=0$ following from the fact that ${\rm cl}^d(0)=0$ and $c_d(0)=0$.

So take $s>0$ and assume the result for all $s'<s$ and all admissible pairs $(V, X^*)$ with $V\subset X$ open, $V\supset X^*$.  Let $U=X\setminus\{x_1\}$, with inclusion $j:U\to X$. By our induction hypothesis, we have
\[
c_d({\rm cl}^d([\sum_{i=2}^sr_i\cdot x_i]))=(-1)^{d-1}(d-1)!\cdot [\sum_{i=2}^sr_i\cdot x_i]\in {\operatorname{CH}}^d(X, X^*).
\]


We have $j^*[x_1]=0$ so 
\[
j^*[\sum_{i=1}^sr_i\cdot [x_i]))=j^*[\sum_{i=2}^sr_i\cdot [x_i]))
\]
and since $j^*\circ c_d\circ {\rm cl}^d=c_d\circ {\rm cl}^d\circ j^*$, we have
\begin{align*}
j^*(c_d({\rm cl}^d&(\sum_{i=1}^sr_i\cdot [x_i]))-(-1)^{d-1}(d-1)!\cdot \sum_{i=1}^sr_i\cdot [x_i])\\
&=(c_d\circ {\rm cl}^d)(j^*(\sum_{i=1}^sr_i\cdot [x_i]))-(-1)^{d-1}(d-1)!\cdot j^*(\sum_{i=1}^sr_i\cdot [x_i])\\
&=(c_d\circ {\rm cl}^d)(j^*(\sum_{i=2}^sr_i\cdot [x_i]))-(-1)^{d-1}(d-1)!\cdot j^*(\sum_{i=2}^sr_i\cdot [x_i])\\
&=j^*(c_d({\rm cl}^d(\sum_{i=2}^sr_i\cdot [x_i]))-(-1)^{d-1}(d-1)!\cdot \sum_{i=2}^sr_i\cdot [x_i])\\
&=0 \in {\operatorname{CH}}^d(U, X^*).
\end{align*}
Via the localization sequence (Lemma~\ref{lem:Localization})
\[
{\mathbb Z}\cdot [x_1]={\operatorname{CH}}_0(x_1)\xrightarrow{i_{x_1*}}{\operatorname{CH}}^d(X, X^*)\xrightarrow{j^*}{\operatorname{CH}}^d(U, X^*)\to 0
\]
we find that  there is an integer $m$ with
\begin{equation}\label{eqn:RRIdentity}
c_d({\rm cl}^d(\sum_{i=1}^sr_i\cdot [x_i]))-(-1)^{d-1}(d-1)!\cdot \sum_{i=1}^sr_i\cdot [x_i]=m\cdot [x_1]\in {\operatorname{CH}}^d(X, X^*),
\end{equation}
and we need to show that $m=0$.


Suppose first that $k$ has characteristic zero. Then $X_{\operatorname{reg}}(d)=X_{\operatorname{sm}}(d)$ and we can use resolution of singularities to give us a projective birational  morphism
\[
p:\tilde{X}\to   X(d)
\]
with $\tilde{X}$  smooth over $k$ and $p$ an isomorphism over $X_{\operatorname{reg}}(d)\supset X\setminus X^*$. Applying Remark~\ref{rem:OpenIm}(2), we have the well-defined pullback map
\[
p^*:{\operatorname{CH}}^d(X, X^*)\to {\operatorname{CH}}^d(\tilde{X}).
\]
with $p^*([x_i])=[y_i]$ if $y_i\in \tilde{X}$ is the closed point $p^{-1}(x_i)$. By Proposition~\ref{prop:ChernClassFunct}(2) and Riemann-Roch on the smooth $k$-scheme $\tilde{X}$, we have
\begin{multline*}
p^*(c_d({\rm cl}^d(\sum_{i=1}^sr_i\cdot [x_i]))-(-1)^{d-1}(d-1)!\cdot \sum_{i=1}^sr_i\cdot [x_i])\\=
c_d({\rm cl}^d(\sum_{i=1}^sr_i\cdot [y_i]))-(-1)^{d-1}(d-1)!\cdot \sum_{i=1}^sr_i\cdot [y_i]=0
\end{multline*}
 Thus 
 \[
0=p^*(c_d({\rm cl}^d(\sum_{i=1}^sr_i\cdot [x_i]))-(-1)^{d-1}(d-1)!\cdot \sum_{i=1}^sr_i\cdot [x_i])=p^*(m[x_1])=m[y_1].
 \]

Let $\pi:\tilde{X}\to {\rm Spec\,} k$ be the structure morphism. Then we have
\[
0=\pi_*(m[y_1])=m[k(y_1):k]\cdot [{\rm Spec\,} k]\in {\operatorname{CH}}_0({\rm Spec\,} k)={\mathbb Z}\cdot [{\rm Spec\,} k]
\]
so $m=0$, and the induction goes through.

In characteristic $p>0$, we use a modification of this argument.\\[5pt]
{\bf Step 1}. We reduce to the case of $k$ finitely generated over ${\mathbb F}_p$. For this, there is a  subfield $k_0$ of $k$, finitely generated over ${\mathbb F}_p$, over which $X, X^*$ and  $x_1,\ldots, x_s\in X\setminus X^*$ are all defined, that is, there is a quasi-projective $k_0$-scheme $X_0$, a closed subset $X^*_0$ of $X_0$ and  closed points $x_{i0}$ of $X_0\setminus X_0^*$ such that
\[
(X_0, X_0^*, x_{10},\ldots, x_{s0})\times_{k_0}k\cong (X, X^*, x_1,\ldots, x_s) 
\]
Let $p_X:X=X_0\times_{k_0}k\to X_0$ be the projection.
 
We claim that ${\operatorname{\rm dim}}_{k_0}X_0={\operatorname{\rm dim}}_kX=d$ and $X_0\setminus X_0^*$ is an admissible pair over $k_0$. This first identity follows from the faithful flatness of $k_0\hookrightarrow k$, more generally, $X_0(i)\times_{k_0}k\cong X(i)$, and thus $X_0^*\supset X_0(\le d-1)$. Similarly, $X(d)^0=X_0(d)^0\times_{k_0}k$ and by faithful flatness again, $X_0(d)^0\times_{k_0}k$ being reduced implies $X_0(d)^0$ is reduced. Take $y_0\in X_0\setminus X^*_0$ and let $y\in X\setminus X^*$ be a point lying over $y_0$,  giving the flat local extension ${\mathcal O}_{X_0,y_0}\to {\mathcal O}_{X, y}$. By \cite[Theorem 23.7]{MatsumuraCRT}, the fact that ${\mathcal O}_{X,y}$ is regular of dimension $d$ implies ${\mathcal O}_{X_0,y_0}$ is regular of dimension $d$, hence $X_0\setminus X_0^*\subset X_{0{\operatorname{reg}}}$. Since $X\setminus X^*$ is dense in $X(d)$, it follows that $X_0\setminus X_0^*$ is dense in  $X_{0{\operatorname{reg}}}$. Thus $(X_0, X_0^*)$ is an admissible pair over $k_0$, as claimed. In particular, we have well-defined pullback maps
\[
p_X^*:{\operatorname{CH}}^d(X_0, X_0^*)\to {\operatorname{CH}}^d(X, X^*),\ p_X^*:F^dK_0(X_0)\to F^dK_0(X).
\]
Since $x_{i0}\times_{k_0}k=x_i$, we have $p_X^*([x_{i0}])=[x_i]\in {\operatorname{CH}}^d(X, X^*)$ and $p_X^*[k(x_{i0})]=[k(x_i)]$ in $F^dK_0(X)$. By Proposition~\ref{prop:ChernClassFunct}(3) (substituting $(k_0, k)$ for $(k, F)$) we have
\[
p_X^*(c_d({\rm cl}^d(\sum_{i=1}^sr_i[x_{i0}]))=c_d({\rm cl}^d(\sum_{i=1}^sr_i[x_i]).
\]
This reduces us to proving the analog of \eqref{eqn:RRIdentity} for $(X_0, X_0^*)$; changing notation, we may assume that $k$ is finitely generated over ${\mathbb F}_p$. \\[5pt]
 {\bf Step 2}. Spreading out.    
   
 As above, we have  the identity \eqref{eqn:RRIdentity} in ${\operatorname{CH}}^d(X, X^*)$. 
 Represent ${\rm cl}^d(\sum_{i=1}^sr_i\cdot [x_i])$ as the $K_0$-class of a perfect complex $E$ on $X$, so 
\[
{\rm cl}^d(\sum_{i=1}^sr_i\cdot [x_i])=[E_{\text{ev}}]-[E_{\text{odd}}]
\]
where $E_{\text{ev}}=\oplus_{i\ge0}E_{2i}$ and $E_{\text{odd}}=\oplus_{i\ge0}E_{2i+1}$.  Taking a morphism
\begin{equation}\label{eqn:RepresentingMorphism}
(f_1, f_2):X\to ({\mathbb P}^{N_1}\times{\operatorname{\rm Gr}}(m_1, M_1))\times({\mathbb P}^{N_2}\times{\operatorname{\rm Gr}}(m_2, M_2))
\end{equation}
with $f_1^*E_{m_1, M_1}(-1)\cong E_{\text{ev}}$ and $f_2^*E_{m_2, M_2}(-1)\cong E_{\text{odd}}$, we have
\[
c_d({\rm cl}^d(\sum_{i=1}^sr_i\cdot [x_i]))=c_d(f_1-f_2):=(f_1, f_2)^*(c_d([p_1^*E_{m_1, M_1}(-1)]-[p_2^*E_{m_2, M_2}(-1)])).
\]

Represent 
\[
c_d([p_{1}^*E_{m_1, M_1}(-1)]-[p_{2}^*E_{m_2, M_2}(-1)])\in {\operatorname{CH}}^d({\mathbb P}^{N_1}\times{\operatorname{\rm Gr}}(m_1, M_1)\times{\mathbb P}^{N_2}\times{\operatorname{\rm Gr}}(m_2, M_2))
\]
by a cycle
\[
C_d\in Z^d({\mathbb P}^{N_1}\times{\operatorname{\rm Gr}}(m_1, M_1)\times{\mathbb P}^{N_2}\times{\operatorname{\rm Gr}}(m_2, M_2)),
\]
so $c_d({\rm cl}^d(\sum_{i=1}^sr_i\cdot [x_i]))$ is represented by the 0-cycle
\[
(f_1, f_2)^*(g\cdot C_d)\in Z^d(X\setminus X^*)
\]
for some $g\in (\operatorname{GL}_{N_1+1}\times\operatorname{GL}_{M_1}\times \operatorname{GL}_{N_2+1}\times\operatorname{GL}_{M_2})(k)$, with $(f_1, f_2)^{-1}({\rm supp}\,(gC_d))$ a finite set of closed points of $X\setminus X^*$. Similarly, the identity
\[
c_d({\rm cl}^d(\sum_{i=1}^sr_i\cdot [x_i]))-(-1)^{d-1}(d-1)!\sum_{i=1}^sr_i\cdot [x_i])=m\cdot [x_1]\in {\operatorname{CH}}^d(X, X^*)
\]
is given by an identity of 0-cycles on $X\setminus X^*$, 
\[
\sum_{j=1}^\ell i_{C_j*}({\operatorname{div}} h_j)=m\cdot x_1 -(f_1, f_2)^*(g\cdot C_d)+(-1)^{d-1}(d-1)!\sum_{i=1}^sr_i\cdot x_i,
\] 
where $i_{C_j}:C_j\to X$ are Cartier curves on $X$ relative to $X^*$ with $h_j\in {\mathcal O}_{C_j:C_j\cap X^*}^\times$. 


Let $U_j\subset C_j$ be the maximal open subset of $C_j$ over which $h_j$ is a regular function. Since $h_j\in {\mathcal O}_{C_j:C_j\cap X^*}^\times$,  $U_j$ contains $C_j\cap X^*$. Thus, letting $T=\cup_{j=1}^\ell i_{C_j}(C_j\setminus U_j)$, $T$ is a finite set of closed points of $X\setminus X^*$. Choose a closed point $r_{ij}$, $i=1,\ldots, q_j$ in each irreducible component of $C_j$, with $i_{C_j}(r_{ij})\in X\setminus X^*$ and let $R=\{i_{C_j}(r_{ij})\mid j=1,\ldots, \ell, i=1\ldots q_j\}$. Let
\[
P=\{x_1,\ldots, x_s\}\cup (f_1, f_2)^{-1}({\rm supp}\,(gC_d))\cup T\cup R.
\]
Then $P$ is a finite set of closed points of $X\setminus X^*\subset X(d)$.

Since $k$ is finitely generated over ${\mathbb F}_p$, we can apply the spreading out method discussed in \S\ref{sec:Spread}. We spread out $(X(d), X^*\cap X(d), P)$ to $({\mathcal X}, {\mathcal X}^*, {\mathcal P})\to {\rm Spec\,} S$ for  a finitely generated ${\mathbb F}_p$-algebra $S$ that is smooth over ${\mathbb F}_p$, with ${\mathcal X}\to {\rm Spec\,} S$ projective, $k$ the quotient field of $S$ and $({\mathcal X}, {\mathcal X}^*, {\mathcal P})\otimes_Sk=(X(d), X^*\cap X(d), P)$. 


We then apply Lemma~\ref{lem:RegularRes} to give  a flat projective $S$-scheme $\tilde{{\mathcal X}}\to {\rm Spec\,} S$ with a projective morphism $q:\tilde{{\mathcal X}}\to {\mathcal X}$ such that $q$ is \'etale over a neighborhood of ${\mathcal P}$ in ${\mathcal X}$, and with $\tilde{{\mathcal X}}$ smooth and quasi-projective of dimension $d+{\operatorname{\rm dim}}_kS$ over ${\mathbb F}_p$. Let $q_k:\tilde{X}\to X(d)$ be the pullback of $q$ over ${\rm Spec\,} k\to {\rm Spec\,} S$. Then $\tilde{X}$ is   projective of pure dimension $d$ over $k$ and is regular,  and  $q_k$ is a projective morphism that is \'etale over a neighborhood of $P$ in $X(d)$. 

In particular, the cycle-theoretic pullbacks $q_k^*((f_1, f_2)^*(g\cdot C_d)), q_k^*(1\cdot x_i)\in Z^d(\tilde{X})$ are  defined. Using Lemma~\ref{lem:PartialFunct} we have
\[
 [q_k^*((f_1, f_2)^*(g\cdot C_d))]-[q_k^*((-1)^{d-1}(d-1)!\sum_{i=1}^sr_ix_i)]=[m\cdot q_k^*(1\cdot x_1)]\in {\operatorname{CH}}^d(\tilde{X}).
 \]
 Using the functoriality of cycle-theoretic pullback (when defined), we have
 \[
 q_k^*((f_1, f_2)^*(g\cdot C_d))=(f_1q_k, f_2q_k)^*(g\cdot C_d).
 \]
 
By the naturality of the Chern class map $c_d:K_0(-)\to {\operatorname{CH}}^d(-)$ as expressed in Remark~\ref{rem:LciPullback} and \eqref{eqn:ChernClassLciPullback2},  we have
 \begin{align*}
[(f_1q_k, f_2q_k)^*(g\cdot C_d))]&=c_d([(f_1q_k)^*E_{m_1, M_1}(-1)]-[(f_2q_k)^*E_{m_2, M_2}(-1)]\\
&=c_d([q_k^*E_\text{ev}]-[q_k^*E_{\text{odd}}])\\
&=c_d({\rm cl}^d([q_k^*(\sum_{i=1}^sr_i\cdot x_i)]))\\
&=(-1)^{d-1}(d-1)![q_k^*(\sum_{i=1}^sr_i\cdot x_i)]\in {\operatorname{CH}}^d(\tilde{X}),
\end{align*}
with this last identity following from Lemma~\ref{lem:GRRReg}. 
Thus 
\begin{align*}
m\cdot [q_k^*(1\cdot x_1)]&= [q_k^*((f_1, f_2)^*(g\cdot C_d))]-[q_k^*((-1)^{d-1}(d-1)!\sum_{i=1}^sr_ix_i]\\
&=[(f_1q_k, f_2q_k)^*(g\cdot C_d)]-(-1)^{d-1}(d-1)![q_k^*(\sum_{i=1}^sr_i\cdot x_i)]\\
&=0\in {\operatorname{CH}}^d(\tilde{X}).
\end{align*}

Let $\pi:\tilde{X}\to {\rm Spec\,} k$ be the structure morphism. Since $q_k^*(1\cdot x_1)$ is a non-zero, effective zero-cycle on the projective $k$-scheme $\tilde{X}$, we have $\pi_*(q_k^*(1\cdot x_1))\neq0\in {\operatorname{CH}}_0({\rm Spec\,} k)={\mathbb Z}$, and we see as before that $m=0$.
<!-- end proof-37 -->
<!-- corollary-1: body_md -->
\label{cor:RR} Let $k$ be an infinite field,  let  $(X, X^*)$, $(X, X')$ be admissible pairs over $k$ and let   $d={\operatorname{\rm dim}}_kX$. Suppose that $X'\subset X^*$. Then the map
\[
j^{X^*, X'}_*:{\operatorname{CH}}^d(X, X^*)\to {\operatorname{CH}}^d(X, X')
\]
induced by the inclusion $X\setminus X^*\subset X\setminus X'$ is surjective with kernel killed by $(d-1)!$.
<!-- end corollary-1 -->
<!-- proof-38: body_md -->
The map $j^{X^*, X'}_*$ is surjective by Lemma~\ref{lem:CHSurj}. We have the commutative diagram
\[
\xymatrix{
{\operatorname{CH}}^d(X, X^*)\ar[r]^{j^{X^*, X'}_*}\ar[dr]_{{\rm cl}^d}&{\operatorname{CH}}^d(X, X')\ar[d]^{{\rm cl}^d}\\
&F^dK_0(X)
}
\]
By Theorem~\ref{thm:RR}, the kernel of ${\rm cl}^d:{\operatorname{CH}}^d(X, X^*)\to F^dK_0(X)$ is killed by $(d-1)!$, so the same holds for the kernel of $j^{X*, X'}_*$.
<!-- end proof-38 -->
<!-- remark-18: body_md -->
We expect that the map $j^{X^*, X'}_*:{\operatorname{CH}}^d(X, X^*)\to {\operatorname{CH}}^d(X, X')$ is an isomorphism for all admissible pairs $(X, X^*)$, $(X, X')$ with  $X'\subset X^*$.
<!-- end remark-18 -->
<!-- proposition-12: body_md -->
\label{prop:RRCH0} The map  
$\prod_{i=0}^{{\operatorname{\rm dim}}_kX}{\rm cl}^i_0$ is surjective. Moreover, suppose $X$ is reduced and 
\[
{\rm codim}_{X(i)}X(i)\cap X(j)\ge 2,\ 0\le i<j\le {\operatorname{\rm dim}}_kX.
\]
Then the kernel of $\prod_{i=0}^{{\operatorname{\rm dim}}_kX}{\rm cl}^i_0$ is killed by $({\operatorname{\rm dim}}_kX-1)!$.
<!-- end proposition-12 -->
<!-- proof-39: body_md -->
Since $Z_0(X\setminus Y^*)=\oplus_{i=0}^{{\operatorname{\rm dim}}_kX}Z^i(X(\le i), X^*(\le i))$, the map 
\eqref{eqn:CH0CH*Comp} is surjective. As ${\rm cl}^i:{\operatorname{CH}}^i(X(\le i), X^*(\le i))\to F^iK_0(X(\le i))$ is surjective for each $i$, the surjectivity of $\prod_{i=0}^{{\operatorname{\rm dim}}_kX}{\rm cl}^i_0$ follows.

In case ${\rm codim}_{X(i)}X(i)\cap X(j)\ge 2$ for all $0\le i<j\le {\operatorname{\rm dim}}_kX$, the map \eqref{eqn:CH0CH*Comp} is an isomorphism (Proposition~\ref{prop:CH0CH*}) and then the second statement follows from Theorem~\ref{thm:RR}.
<!-- end proof-39 -->
<!-- remark-19: body_md -->
The inclusion $\iota_{\le i}:X(\le i)\to X$ induces a pullback map
\[
\iota_{\le i}^*:F_0K_0(X)\to F^iK_0(X(\le i))
\]
and 
\[
\oplus_{i=0}^{{\operatorname{\rm dim}}_kX}\iota_{\le i}^*:F_0K_0(X)\to \oplus_{i=0}^{{\operatorname{\rm dim}}_k X}F^iK_0(X(\le i))
\]
 is surjective. However, it is not clear that Proposition~\ref{prop:RRCH0} sheds any light on the exponent of the kernel of ${\rm cl}_0:{\operatorname{CH}}_0(X, Y^*)\to F_0K_0(X)$ in case $X$ is not equi-dimensional, even under the hypotheses of Proposition~\ref{prop:RRCH0}.
<!-- end remark-19 -->
<!-- ex-2: body_md -->
Consider the case $X={\rm Spec\,} k[x,y,z]/(z(x,y))$, $Y=\{(0,0,0)\}$ discussed in Example~\ref{ex:CH0}. It is not hard to show that $F_0K_0(X)=0$: if $p\neq (0,0,0)$ is a closed point in the $z$-axis, with defining ideal $(f_p(z))\subset k[z]$, then as $f_p(0)$ is in $k^\times$, we can extend $f_p(z)$ to a regular function $\tilde{f}_p(x,y,z)\in k[x,y,z]/(z(x,y))$ with restriction to the $x$-$y$-plane the constant function with value $f_p(0)$. Then $\tilde{f}_p(x,y,z)$ is a unit on $X\setminus\{p\}$, hence a non-zero divisor in $k[x,y,z]/(z(x,y))$, giving the exact sequence
\[
0\to {\mathcal O}_X\xrightarrow{\times \tilde{f}_p}{\mathcal O}_X\to k(p)\to 0,
\]
showing that $[k(p)]=0$ in $K_0(X)$. Similarly, for $q\neq(0,0,0)$ a closed point in the $x$-$y$-plane, we also have $[k(q)]=0$ in $K_0(X)$, so $F_0K_0(X)=0$. 

On the other hand, we have computed
\[
{\operatorname{CH}}_0(X, Y^*)=Z_0(z\text{-axis}\setminus\{(0,0,0)\})
\]
so ${\rm cl}_0:{\operatorname{CH}}_0(X, Y^*)\to F_0K_0(X)$ has kernel the free abelian group on the closed points of ${\mathbb A}^1_k\setminus\{0\}$, a free abelian group whose rank is the cardinality of $k$ (since we are assuming $k$ is an infinite field). 

In \cite{GK}, Gupta-Krishna use the modification ${\operatorname{CH}}_0^{\text{BK}}(X, Y^*)$ of ${\operatorname{CH}}_0(X, Y^*)$ defined by Binda-Krishna in \cite[\S 3.3]{BindaKrishna},  using finite morphisms $f:C\to X$ with $C$ of dimension one and $f$ an lci morphism over a neighborhood of $Y^*\cap f(C)$ in $X$ instead of taking $f$ to be a closed immersion. The same analysis as for ${\operatorname{CH}}_0(X, Y^*)$ in the above example gives 
\[
{\operatorname{CH}}_0^{\text{BK}}(X, Y^*)=Z_0(z\text{-axis}\setminus\{(0,0,0)\})=Z_0({\mathbb A}^1_k\setminus\{0\}),
\]
for $k$ an arbitrary field. This says that the result  \cite[Theorem 8.1(1), (2)]{GK} for $X$ a geometrically reduced affine scheme of finite type over a field $k$ should add the hypothesis that $X$ is equi-dimensional over $k$.
<!-- end ex-2 -->
<!-- remark-20: body_md -->
\label{rem:FultonChernClass}
We have the  Chow groups ${\operatorname{CH}}_m(Y)$ of algebraic cycles of dimension $m$ (over $k$) modulo rational equivalence. We will use Fulton's Chern class operators  \cite[\S 3.2, Example 3.2.7]{Fulton}
\[
c_n^F(-)\cap -:K_0(Y)\to {\rm Hom}_{\mathbb Z}({\operatorname{CH}}_m(Y)\to {\operatorname{CH}}_{m-n}(Y))
\]
Assuming $Y$ is equi-dimensional of dimension $d$ over $k$, we can index the Chow groups by codimension, giving
\[
c_n^F(-)\cap -:K_0(Y)\to {\rm Hom}_{\mathbb Z}({\operatorname{CH}}^m(Y)\to {\operatorname{CH}}^{m+n}(Y))
\]
and we have
\[
c_n^F(-)\cap [Y]:K_0(Y)\to {\operatorname{CH}}^n(Y)
\]
where $[Y]\in {\operatorname{CH}}^0(Y)$ is the fundamental class: if $Y$ has integral components $Y_1,\ldots, Y_r$, then $[Y]$ is the class of $\sum_{i=1}^r1\cdot Y_i$ in ${\operatorname{CH}}_{{\operatorname{\rm dim}}_kY}(Y)$. 

If $Y$ is smooth over $k$, the Chern class map defined following Grothendieck's method \cite{Grothendieck}
\[
c_n(-):K_0(Y)\to {\operatorname{CH}}^n(Y)
\]
satisfies
\[
c_n(x)=c_n^F(x)\cap[Y]\in {\operatorname{CH}}^n(Y);
\]
see \cite[\S 3.2, Example 3.2.7]{Fulton}. We will therefore often  write $c_n(x)$ for $c_n^F(x)\cap [Y]$ for $Y$ equi-dimensional over $k$. Given a smooth spreading out ${\mathcal Y}\to {\rm Spec\,} S$ of $Y$, we will use the same notation replacing $Y$ with ${\mathcal Y}$, viewing ${\mathcal Y}$ as a smooth quasi-projective ${\mathbb F}_p$-scheme.
<!-- end remark-20 -->
<!-- lemma-23: body_md -->
\label{lem:GRRReg} Let $k$ be a finitely generated field extension of ${\mathbb F}_p$, and take $Y\in {\operatorname{\mathbf{Sch}}}_k^{{\operatorname{\text{\rm qp}}}}$. Suppose $Y$ is equi-dimensional over $k$ and regular. Let $Z\subset Y$ be an integral closed subscheme of codimension $m$, giving the corresponding elements $[Z]\in {\operatorname{CH}}^m(Y)$, $[{\mathcal O}_Z]\in K_0(Y)$.   Then
\[
c_n^F([{\mathcal O}_Z])\cap[Y]=\begin{cases} 0 &\text{ for }n<m,\\ (-1)^{m-1}(m-1)![Z]&\text{ for }n=m.\end{cases}
\]
<!-- end lemma-23 -->
<!-- proof-40: body_md -->
Since $k$ is finitely generated over ${\mathbb F}_p$, there is  a  spreading out $({\mathcal Y}, {\mathcal Z})\to {\rm Spec\,} S$ of $(Y, Z)$. Since ${\mathcal Y}$ is of finite type over ${\mathbb F}_p$, the regular locus in ${\mathcal Y}$ is open, and by assumption contains $Y$. Thus, after inverting a non-zero element of  $S$ if necessary, we may assume the ${\mathcal Y}$ is regular. Since ${\mathbb F}_p$ is perfect, this implies that ${\mathcal Y}$ is smooth over ${\mathbb F}_p$, hence ${\mathcal Y}\to {\rm Spec\,} S$ is a smooth spreading out of $Y$. 

We may assume that  ${\mathcal Z}\subset {\mathcal Y}$ is an integral codimension $m$ closed subscheme of ${\mathcal Y}$, again after localizing $S$ further if necessary. Let $j:Y\to {\mathcal Y}$ be the inclusion, a flat morphism. Then as $c_n^F(-)\cap-$ is functorial for flat morphisms \cite[Theorem 3.2]{Fulton}, we have
\[
j^*(c_n^F([{\mathcal O}_{\mathcal Z}])\cap[{\mathcal Y}])=c_n^F([{\mathcal O}_Z])\cap[Y].
\]
Since ${\mathcal Y}$ is smooth over ${\mathbb F}_p$, we have
\[
c_n^F([{\mathcal O}_{\mathcal Z}])\cap[{\mathcal Y}]=c_n([{\mathcal O}_{\mathcal Z}])\in {\operatorname{CH}}^n({\mathcal Y}),
\]
and by Grothendieck-Riemann-Roch for the smooth quasi-projective ${\mathbb F}_p$-scheme ${\mathcal Y}$ \cite[Example 15.3.1]{Fulton}, we have
\[
c_n([{\mathcal O}_{\mathcal Z}])=\begin{cases} 0 &\text{ for }n<m,\\ (-1)^{m-1}(m-1)![{\mathcal Z}]&\text{ for }n=m,\end{cases}
\]
where $[{\mathcal Z}]\in {\operatorname{CH}}^m({\mathcal Y})$ is the class of the integral closed subscheme ${\mathcal Z}$. But since $j^*([{\mathcal Z}])=[Z]$, the lemma is a consequence of these three identities.
<!-- end proof-40 -->
<!-- lemma-24: body_md -->
\label{lem:RegularRes} There exists a smooth quasi-projective ${\mathbb F}_p$-scheme ${\mathcal Y}\to {\rm Spec\,} {\mathbb F}_p$ and a morphism $q:{\mathcal Y}\to {\mathcal X}$ over ${\mathbb F}_p$ such that\\[5pt]
1. $q$ is proper and generically finite\\[2pt]
2. $q$ is \'etale over a neighborhood of $P\subset {\mathcal P}$\\[2pt]
3. After localizing $S$ is necessary, ${\mathcal Y}\to {\rm Spec\,} S$ is flat\\[5pt]
Moreover, if $X$ is projective over $k$, we may take  ${\mathcal Y}$ to be projective over   ${\rm Spec\,} S$ and over ${\mathcal X}$.
<!-- end lemma-24 -->
<!-- proof-41: body_md -->
Since ${\mathcal X}\setminus {\mathcal X}^*$ is of finite type over ${\mathbb F}_p$, the regular locus of  ${\mathcal X}\setminus {\mathcal X}^*$ is an open subscheme, containing the regular scheme $X\setminus X^*$. Thus,  after localizing $S$ if necessary, we may assume that ${\mathcal X}\setminus {\mathcal X}^*$ is regular. Since ${\mathbb F}_p$ is perfect, this implies that ${\mathcal X}\setminus {\mathcal X}^*$ is smooth over ${\mathbb F}_p$. Similarly, we may assume that ${\mathcal P}\subset {\mathcal X}\setminus {\mathcal X}^*$. For each $i=1,\ldots, r$ choose a closed point $x_i\in \mathfrak{p}_i$, so $x_i$ is in the smooth locus of ${\mathcal X}$ over ${\mathbb F}_p$.

By \cite[Theorem 1.1, Theorem 2.6]{BhattSnowden}, there is a smooth, finite-type ${\mathbb F}_p$-scheme ${\mathcal Y}$ and a proper morphism $q:{\mathcal Y}\to {\mathcal X}$ that is generically finite and is \'etale over a neighborhood of $\{x_0,\ldots, x_r\}$. The points (1), (2), (3) follow from this. 

  
 
  In case $X\to {\rm Spec\,} k$ is projective, ${\mathcal X}\to {\rm Spec\,} S$ is projective by construction, say ${\mathcal X}$ is a closed subscheme of ${\mathbb P}^N_S$. Let $\overline{{\rm Spec\,} S}\subset {\mathbb P}^M_{{\mathbb F}_p}$ be a projective closure of the 
 finite-type affine ${\mathbb F}_p$-scheme ${\rm Spec\,} S$, and let 
 \[
 \overline{{\mathcal X}}\subset {\mathbb P}^N_{{\mathbb P}^M_{{\mathbb F}_p}}={\mathbb P}^N_{{\mathbb F}_p}\times_{{\mathbb F}_p}{\mathbb P}^M_{{\mathbb F}_p}\subset {\mathbb P}^{NM-1}_{{\mathbb F}_p}
 \]
 be the closure of ${\mathcal X}$. Applying the Bhatt-Snowden construction as above to $\overline{{\mathcal X}}$ gives us $\overline{{\mathcal Y}}\to \overline{{\mathcal X}}$, and  since $\overline{{\mathcal X}}$ is proper over ${\mathbb F}_p$, 
  \cite[Theorem 2.6]{BhattSnowden} tells us that we can take $\overline{{\mathcal Y}}$ to be projective over ${\mathbb F}_p$. But then $\overline{{\mathcal Y}}\to \overline{{\mathcal X}}$ is a projective morphism, so pulling back over ${\rm Spec\,} S\hookrightarrow {\mathbb P}^M_{{\mathbb F}_p}$ gives ${\mathcal Y}\to {\mathcal X}\to {\rm Spec\,} S$ with ${\mathcal Y}\to {\rm Spec\,} S$ and ${\mathcal Y}\to {\mathcal X}$ projective.
<!-- end proof-41 -->
<!-- remark-21: body_md -->
\label{rem:LciPullback} Let $Y$ be quasi-projective  and  equi-dimensional over $k$, and let $f:Y\to H$ be a morphism to a smooth quasi-projective $k$-scheme $H$. Take $x\in K_0(H)$. Since $H$ is smooth over $k$, the morphism $f$ is an lci morphism, so we have a well-defined lci pullback map \cite[\S 6.6]{Fulton}
\[
f^!:{\operatorname{CH}}_n(H)\to {\operatorname{CH}}_{n-c}(Y)
\]
where $c={\operatorname{\rm dim}}_kH-{\operatorname{\rm dim}}_kY$; if $Y$ is regular, we write this as
\[
f^*:{\operatorname{CH}}^*(H)\to {\operatorname{CH}}^*(Y).
\]

For $\alpha\in {\operatorname{CH}}_r(H)$,  $m>0$ an integer and $x\in K_0(H)$, we have
\begin{equation}\label{eqn:BivChernClass}
f^!(c_m^F(x)\cap \alpha)=c_m^F(f^*(x))\cap f^!(\alpha).
\end{equation}
Indeed, we have the bivariant class in ${\operatorname{CH}}^*(H=H)$ by  $(Z\xrightarrow{g}H, y\in {\operatorname{CH}}_r(Z))\mapsto c_m^F(g^*x)\cap y$ (see \cite[\S17.3, pg. 325]{Fulton}), and  $f^!$ defines a bivariant class in ${\operatorname{CH}}^*(Y\to H)$, via $(g:Z\to H, y\in {\operatorname{CH}}_r(Z))\mapsto f^!(y)\in {\operatorname{CH}}_{r-c}(Z\times_HY)$. Then \eqref{eqn:BivChernClass} follows from \cite[Proposition 17.3.2]{Fulton} applied to $c=f^!$. In particular, taking $\alpha=[H]$ and assuming $Y$ is regular, we have
\begin{equation}\label{eqn:ChernClassLciPullback}
f^*(c_m(x))=c_m(f^*(x))\in {\operatorname{CH}}^m(Y)
\end{equation}

If now $c_m(x)$ is represented by some $z\in Z^m(H)$ such that $f^{-1}({\rm supp}\,(z))$ has pure codimension $m$ in $Y$, then the cycle-theoretic pullback $f^*(z)\in Z^m(Y)$ is defined and we have
\begin{equation}\label{eqn:ChernClassLciPullback2}
c_m(f^*(x))=[f^*(z)]\in {\operatorname{CH}}^m(Y).
\end{equation}
<!-- end remark-21 -->
